documents.body:
# Architecture

This chapter covers how packs work under the hood: loading, dependency sharing, generated files, and the build pipeline. You don't need this to write a pack, but it helps when debugging or doing advanced work.
documents.name: architecture / Architecture

documents.section: Architecture / App environment and data directory
documents.body:
## App environment and data directory

Every process resolves its environment and data paths through `resolveAppEnvironment()` (`@apackdev/sdk/env`).

- **Environment:** `production`, `beta`, `development` or `test`. The Electron main process decides it once: Playwright runs are `test`, packaged builds use the channel stamped at build time, and source runs use `APACK_ENV` or default to `development`. It passes `APACK_ENV` and `APACK_USER_DATA_DIR` to the API process. A process that gets neither, and isn't given `{ env }`, throws; nothing falls back to production.
- **Data directory:** `APACK_USER_DATA_DIR` if set, otherwise the platform's app data dir for the environment's app name (`apack`, `apack-beta`, `apack-dev`, `apack-test`). On macOS that is `~/Library/Application Support/<appName>`.

| Path under the data dir | Contents |
|---|---|
| `packs/` | Installed packs, one directory per pack id — every pack, the ones the app ships included |
| `installed-packs.json` | Installed packs' install state and their `enabled` state |
| `ears-db/` | The elmdb database the engine's data is kept in |
| `run-history/` | The run history's elmdb database: every flow run's nodes, kept 30 days |
| `secrets.json` | API keys: metadata plain, values encrypted |
| `media/` | Media assets |
| `api-port` | The API's port (development only) |
| `api-token` | The token the API requires, for local tools (development only, readable only by you) |

CLI commands pass `{ env }` explicitly: `apack pack install`/`apack pack uninstall`/`apack pack list` target production unless given `--profile development` (development) or `--profile beta` (beta).
documents.name: architecture / Architecture / App environment and data directory

documents.body:
## Layers

The app is built from packages whose imports point down only (`npm run check:specifiers` fails on an upward import):

| Package | Holds | Imports |
|---|---|---|
| `@apackdev/ears` | The EARS engine (`createEarsEngine`), its types, the database port; `@apackdev/ears/lmdb`, which opens elmdb databases | No `@apackdev/*` package |
| `@apackdev/sdk` | The pack contract and pack runtime: the lookups of what packs registered, service contracts, event sends, logging and error reports over the bound bus, the SDK entities and their repositories, the `HostRuntime` port | `@apackdev/ears` |
| `@apackdev/host` (private) | The app runtime: the five app services (`/services`), the app's own state (`/app-state`), the registered packs and pack runtime (`/packs`, `/packs/runtime`), the bus (`/bus`), migrations (`/migrations`), API keys (`/secrets`) | `@apackdev/sdk`, `@apackdev/ears` |
| `packages/api` | Transport (`node:http`, `ws`, tRPC routers, the log stream), process boot and composition | All of the above |
| `packages/renderer` | The frontend composition: binds the frontend port | |

Packs import `@apackdev/sdk`, `@apackdev/ears` and `@apackdev/ui`, never `@apackdev/host`. What an app owns is an instance its composition root creates and binds: the engine, the registered packs (`createPackRegistry()`, and in the renderer `createFePackRegistry()`) and the host services. No SDK, EARS or host module keeps them at module scope.

documents.body: ## Pack loading lifecycle
documents.name: architecture / Architecture / Pack loading lifecycle

documents.body:
### Install

`apack pack install` (or the Packs view) installs into the data dir's `packs/<id>/`. An installed pack has the pack layout, the same layout as `apack pack build`'s `dist/` and the release archive:

```
<id>/
  apack.json          # The pack's manifest, as written
  integrity.json          # Format version, versions, provenance, sha256 of every file
  runtime/
    index.cjs          # Backend: exports `registration` and `setCompiledDir`
    fe.js              # Frontend entry
    fe.css             # Extracted styles
    content/             # Compiled content
  build/               # Build-time code dependents load (step build facets, content runtime)
  types/
    snapshot.json      # Types, manifest, SDK version, flow helpers for dependents' codegen
```

Installing is stage, verify, place:

1. **Stage:** a built pack source is copied into a temporary staging directory (`runtime/`, `build/`, `types/` from `dist/`, without source maps), carrying the verified producer manifest and expected file hashes; staging does not re-sign arbitrary copied bytes. An archive — `.tgz` or `.zip` — is checked against its sha256 before anything is unpacked. A GitHub install takes that checksum from the release's `<archive>.sha256` asset and refuses a release that publishes none; a URL install has one only if the caller passes it, and warns when it doesn't. Downloads carry a two-minute timeout, so a stalled one fails instead of hanging the install.
2. **Verify:** the pack's format version must match the host's, and the files on disk must be exactly the ones `integrity.json` lists, with matching checksums.
3. **Place:** the staged pack is copied into a hidden `.<id>.installing-<pid>-…` dir in `packs/`, the current copy (if any) is renamed aside to `.<id>.previous-…`, the new copy is renamed into place, and the previous one is removed. At boot, `prepareHostDataDirs` restores a pack whose install crashed between those renames, unless the pack was uninstalled since, and removes stale staging dirs (a dir whose process is gone, or which predates the boot).

The source directory must be built first: installing a directory with neither a `integrity.json` nor a `dist/runtime/index.cjs` beside `dist/types/snapshot.json` fails and asks you to run `apack pack build`. A directory in `packs/` that isn't a pack layout is skipped at boot with a warning.

documents.section: Architecture / Pack loading lifecycle / Backend boot
documents.body:
### Backend boot

`setupBackend()` in `packages/api/src/setup/backend.ts` runs, in order. The API holds only transport, process boot and this composition: the app runtime it calls lives in `@apackdev/host` (pack loading, lifecycle, reload and writing in `@apackdev/host/packs/runtime`, the migrations runners in `@apackdev/host/migrations`, the bus in `@apackdev/host/bus`).

0. Opens the app's data and binds the app (`openAppStore()`): it creates the app's registered packs (`createPackRegistry()` from `@apackdev/host/packs`), which the SDK's lookups read once bound, and the rest of the steps register into it.
1. Registers the host `packs` system.
2. `prepareHostDataDirs`: records the app version in the data dir (for `apack pack install`) and recovers staging dirs in `packs/`.
3. `forwardSecretsChanges` (`@apackdev/host/secrets`): every system that takes `SECRETS_CHANGED` hears that API key changes, never their values.
4. Installs the packs the app ships into `packs/<id>`, each being a directory under `SHIPPED_PACKS_DIR` that holds an `apack.json`. Missing defaults are installed unless deliberately suppressed. Existing user-managed replacements are preserved; explicitly app-managed copies refresh when the shipped source revision changes. This is before loading, not beside it: a pack is loaded from `packs/`, so it has to be there to be found.
5. Loads packs — one path for all of them, the ones the app ships included. Discovered in `packs/` and reconciled with `installed-packs.json` (new packs added enabled, missing ones removed), the shipped ones ordered first so a pack depending on one finds it registered. For each enabled pack: `hostVersion` check, pack layout format check, a warning on an SDK major version mismatch, and `runtime/index.cjs` loaded from its own installed directory through the module bridge. A pack with no built runtime, or one whose load throws, has a load problem recorded and the rest load. Each pack's systems register as `<packId>/<featureId>`, and the registry's `registerPack()` stores each registration (see [Collision detection](#collision-detection)). A pack contributes only through its registration: nothing registers when its modules are imported.
7. Wires each pack's `onShutdown` hook, keyed by pack id.
8. Logs the database's size on disk and the heap. There is no load step: the engine has read the database from the moment it opened, and an entity type is checked when a write or query names it, after every pack has registered.
9. Runs every pack's `onInit`.
10. Runs app migrations (`runAppMigrations`: the host's own, then the built-in packs', against the app version), then external pack migrations (`runPackMigrations`, each against its own pack version).
11. Content: each built-in pack's declarative `content.sources`, then external packs' compiled content, skipped when a pack's content revision hasn't changed.
12. Starts the bus actor (`createAppBus(registry)` from `@apackdev/host/bus`), which spawns every registered system.
documents.name: architecture / Architecture / Pack loading lifecycle / Backend boot

documents.section: Architecture / Pack loading lifecycle / Frontend boot
documents.body:
### Frontend boot

Every pack's frontend is loaded at runtime, the ones the app ships included. A dev server serves a local pack's from its source instead (`virtual:dev-pack-frontends`), which is what lets a component edit patch in place:

1. Each time this window's bus subscription is established, the application actor queries the loaded packs (`trpc.packs.loaded`), which lists each loaded external pack's `feEntry` and `feStyles` — the pack's `runtime/fe.js` and `runtime/fe.css`, when it has them. It loads only the packs it hasn't loaded yet, so a query that fails leaves them to the next connection and a pack is never loaded twice.
2. For each external pack, the shell loads its frontend (`createPackFrontends(io, packs).load` in `@apackdev/host/fe`, over the window's `importModule` and stylesheet I/O):
   - loads `pack://<id>/builds/<revision>/runtime/fe.css` as a `<link>` when the pack has styles;
   - imports `pack://<id>/builds/<revision>/runtime/fe.js` and registers its default export, a `PackFERegistration`, in the renderer's frontend registry (`createFePackRegistry()` from `@apackdev/host/fe`, bound with `bindFeHost`);
   - returns the surfaces it exports, `[]` when the load failed, or `null` for a pack without frontend code.
3. When it returns surfaces (even none), the shell handles `PACK_FRONTEND_LOADED`, which spawns the surfaces whose ids aren't taken and calls `trpc.bus.packClientReady({ packId })`.
4. `packClientReady` sends the pack's systems `CLIENT_CONNECTED` and asks them to publish, so they send their startup data once the surface actors exist.

A connection's own `CLIENT_CONNECTED` skips the systems of external packs with frontend code (the bus asks `getPacksWithClientLoadedFrontends()`). When the renderer's bus subscription (re)connects, `BUS_SUBSCRIBED` calls `packClientReady` again for every pack whose frontend it loaded. Systems of packs without frontend code are told and asked directly.

A reconnect re-accepts every pack frontend and replaces each surface's actor, so the surface remounts: what the old
connection left unanswered goes with the old actor, and the surface asks again on its new one's `SURFACE_STARTED`.
State a component holds in a `ref` goes too. Hold what the user has typed and not saved in `useSurfaceDraft(name,
initial)` (`@apackdev/sdk/fe`) instead: it is kept by the surface's ref, so the remounted component is handed the same
value. It lasts as long as the window; what must outlive an app restart is saved.

documents.section: Architecture / Pack loading lifecycle / Activation, teardown and reload
documents.body:
### Activation, teardown and reload

The `packs` system handles install, uninstall, enable/disable and update from the Packs view:

- **Activate** (after install or update, or on enable): reads the pack's manifest, loads and registers it, registers `onShutdown`, runs `onInit`, then the pack's pending migrations and its content (skipped when its compiled content are unchanged), sends the bus `PACK_CHANGED` so running systems refresh what they read from packs, then `ACTIVATE_PACK` to spawn its systems. The renderer hears `PACK_ACTIVATED` and asks the application actor to load the frontends it hasn't, the new pack's included. The bus asks a pack's systems to publish right away only for a pack without frontend code; otherwise it waits for `packClientReady`. An install or update that activated but failed to apply reports the content error.
- **Teardown** (before uninstall or update, or on disable): runs the pack's shutdown hooks, unregisters it (registration keeps the event types `bus.send` accepts current), clears its modules from the require cache, and sends the bus `TEARDOWN_PACK` to stop its systems. The renderer hears `PACK_DEACTIVATED`, unregisters the pack's FE extensions, removes its stylesheets and unloads its surfaces.
- **Reload** (development, `POST /dev/reload` on the API from `apack pack dev` or a built-in pack's watch build; a development or test app takes it only with the API token, handled by `reloadPackById` in `@apackdev/host/packs/runtime`, which asks the registry which directory the pack came from): loads and registers the rebuilt runtime before shutting the running one down. If the fresh runtime fails to load or register, the running pack is re-registered and stays as it was. Otherwise the old shutdown hooks run, the new `onShutdown` registers, `onInit` runs, external packs run their pending migrations and re-apply, and the bus `RELOAD_PACK` stops the old and new system ids and starts those still registered, then sends them `CLIENT_CONNECTED` and asks them to publish; `PACK_CHANGED` and its ask follow for every running system. Teardown (disable, uninstall) sends it too, after stopping the pack's systems.

An external pack's migrations run at boot, on activation and on reload, each against the pack's own version; the app's run at boot and after a reset or backup import.

documents.body:
### Collision detection

The host refuses conflicting active ownership before publishing registry lookups:

| What | Checked against |
|---|---|
| Pack id | Registered packs |
| Entity types, relation kinds | Other owners; SDK-owned declarations are refused |
| Step wire types | Other active pack owners; facets from different packs do not merge |
| Service keys | Other packs' keys and the host's services |
| Designations | Other packs' roles |
| Reference identities | Other declaring features, naming both owners |
| Tiptap extension names | Other groups, naming both owners |
| Content writers | Other packs' writers for the same entity type |
| Content appliers | Other appliers for the same content key in the pack |
| Commands | Other packs' command names |

Artifacts, blocks, app-extension slots and DSL keys retain registration-order precedence; removing an
owner reveals contributions from earlier owners. Settings use pack/group or fully qualified feature identities. Writes and resets obey declared dependency
access and opt-in owner restrictions. Registry publication is separate from runtime activation: preserving
an accepted lookup view does not undo arbitrary effects of executable pack code.
documents.name: architecture / Architecture / Entry contracts / Collision detection

documents.body:
## The `pack://` protocol

The installed asset protocol binds every request to an accepted build:

```
pack://<packId>/builds/<buildRevision>/<filePath>
```

The main process verifies the requested build and file receipt under that pack's installed directory.
Traversal and requests without a build revision are refused. A development frontend uses the explicit
source delivery supplied by the host; it does not change installed protocol identity or declaration
checks. The renderer uses revision URLs for built frontend entries, styles and assets.
documents.name: architecture / Architecture / The `pack://` protocol

documents.section: Architecture / Host dependency sharing / Frontend: an import map
documents.body:
### Frontend: an import map

Packs share runtime dependencies with the host, which is critical for correctness — modules with internal state (Vue's reactivity system, XState's actor registry, the SDK's bound frontend host, which its lookups read) must be singletons. The sharing is done by **resolution**: a pack's bundle keeps the bare specifier, and the document's import map resolves it to the host's module.

**Host side (Vite):** each shared module is an entry of the renderer's build, and the plugin injects an import map naming them ahead of the app's own script:

```html
<script type="importmap">
{ "imports": {
  "vue": "./assets/shared-vue-CwIGn1C6.js",
  "@apackdev/sdk/fe": "./assets/shared-apack-sdk-fe-DY7mM_D0.js",
  "@tiptap/pm/model": "./assets/shared-prosemirror-model-YOzlPTVh.js"
} }
</script>
```

In a dev server the targets are the URLs Vite serves those modules at instead (`/node_modules/.vite/deps/vue.js?v=…`, or `/@fs/…` for a workspace package), so the same mechanism covers both.

**Pack side (Vite):** `packExternalsPlugin` leaves every shared specifier **external**, so the pack's bundle emits it untouched:

```javascript
// import { ref } from 'vue'  stays exactly that in dist/runtime/fe.js
import { ref } from 'vue';
```

Because the pack imports the real module rather than a copy of its names, what it gets is a live binding, and an import of a name this apack does not have fails when the module links — naming the export — instead of arriving as `undefined`.

#### Shared third-party deps

`vue`, `xstate`, `@xstate/vue`, `@tiptap/core`, `@tiptap/vue-3`, `@tiptap/starter-kit`, `reka-ui`, `lucide-vue-next`, `@vue-flow/core`, and every subpath of `@tiptap/pm` and `@tiptap/vue-3`

#### Shared SDK modules

`@apackdev/sdk/fe`, `@apackdev/sdk/runtime`, `@apackdev/sdk/steps`, `@apackdev/sdk/artifacts`, `@apackdev/sdk/blocks`, `@apackdev/sdk/designations`, `@apackdev/sdk/events` (`sdkEvents`), `@apackdev/sdk/helpers`, and every `@apackdev/ui` export

#### Deep subpath imports

Only registered barrel subpaths are externalized. Other SDK modules resolve and bundle: the file is compiled into your pack's `fe.js`. The FE build fails if a bundled SDK module needs the app's binding (`bindHost`/`bindFeHost` in `@apackdev/sdk/runtime`), since a bundled copy has nothing bound.

#### `@apackdev/ui`

Components, editors and UI composables (`@apackdev/ui/design/button`, `@apackdev/ui/components/tiptap/TiptapEditor`, `@apackdev/ui/composables/useDebounce`) come from the separate `@apackdev/ui` package. Add it to your pack's dependencies when your UI uses them; backend-only packs don't install it or its editor libraries. The package ships compiled JS with declarations, so component props typecheck with plain `tsc`.

At runtime your pack uses the app's copy: `apack pack build` turns `@apackdev/ui` imports into references to the modules the app exposes, the same way it handles the shared SDK modules. Your `fe.js` stays small, and stateful modules (the Monaco configuration, editor extensions) have one instance across the app. `@apackdev/ui` changes follow semver, and your pack's `hostVersion` states which apps it runs in.

To ship your own copy instead, set `build.bundleUi` in `apack.json`. All of `@apackdev/ui` is then bundled into `fe.js`, so the pack never mixes its copy with the app's.
documents.name: architecture / Architecture / Host dependency sharing / Frontend: an import map

documents.section: Architecture / Host dependency sharing / Backend: the module bridge
documents.body:
### Backend: the module bridge

The API bundles its own copy of `@apackdev/sdk`, `@apackdev/ears` and `@apackdev/host`. Pack runtime code loaded from disk would otherwise get separate instances, with no app bound: no registered packs to look up and no installed EARS engine. `@apackdev/sdk` and `@apackdev/ears` are the shared-instance packages (`SHARED_INSTANCE_PACKAGES` in `@apackdev/host/build/shared-deps`): the bundler externals, this bridge and the test harness's all derive from that one list.

`withHostResolution(fn)` (`packages/apack-host/src/packs/runtime/bridge.ts`) runs a `require()` of pack code through `withModuleBridge()` (`@apackdev/host/packs`), which:

- puts the loader's instances (the API bundle's, in the app) of the bridged `@apackdev/sdk`, `@apackdev/ears` modules (every backend export of the shared-instance packages, except `@apackdev/ears/lmdb`, which only the app loads) in the require cache, and patches `Module._resolveFilename` so those specifiers resolve to them;
- resolves the shared backend packages (`xstate`, `zod`) from the API, since an installed pack has no `node_modules`;
- restores the resolver afterwards. The bridged modules stay cached, so requires the pack makes later get them too.

The pack test harness uses the same bridge with the pack's own SDK instance.
documents.name: architecture / Architecture / Host dependency sharing / Backend: the module bridge

documents.body:
## Host services

The SDK reaches the running app through one typed port, `HostRuntime` (`@apackdev/sdk/runtime`),
bound once per process with `bindHost`. It supplies the event transport, EARS engine, registered packs,
app version and host service implementations. `createHostRuntime(...)` in `@apackdev/host/services`
assembles it; `setupBackend()` in `packages/api/src/runtime/index.ts` opens and binds the app store.
Packs receive their accepted service selection rather than this internal port: logger, emitter,
repository and caller-bound settings are implicit; onboarding, app data, run history, inference,
secrets and filesystem require `consumes.services` declarations. Onboarding is separate from app data.
Reset clears stored data and keys, then runs `onInit`, app-line migrations, pack-line migrations and
content application in dependency order, as startup does. Failed app-line migrations stop later stages.

Sends, logging and error reports are SDK code over the bound bus: `sendToSystem` emits an incoming event, `broadcastToSurface` (and `services.emitter.broadcastToSurface`) goes through the bus actor, which drops it until a client connects, like a system's `emit`, and `createLogger` emits log events, which the API prints once and streams to the logs surface (with nothing bound, as in the CLI, a logger writes to the console). In the renderer, `bindFeHost` binds the application actor, the secrets client behind `secretsClient` (the Settings → Secrets procedures) and a transport that sends to systems over the API client. Using the port with nothing bound throws, naming `bindHost` or `bindFeHost`.

A pack can't register a service under a host service's name.
documents.name: architecture / Architecture / Host services

documents.body:
## Secrets store

The user's API keys live in `@apackdev/host/secrets`, which is host-only and not part of `HostRuntime`.

- `secrets.json` holds each key's metadata in plain text and its value encrypted with AES-256-GCM.
- The data key is kept in a `KeyVault`: the OS credential store (`@napi-rs/keyring`), or a `secrets.key` file in the test environment, in development with `APACK_SECRETS_VAULT=file`, or after the user allows unprotected storage.
- Values enter only through the API's `secrets.*` tRPC procedures, never the event bus. Inference reads a provider's selected key with `secretsStore.keyFor(provider)`.
- Packs see metadata only, through `services.secrets` (list, select, rename, delete).
documents.name: architecture / Architecture / Secrets store

documents.body:
## Persistence

The app keeps two [elmdb](https://github.com/spankyed/elmdb) databases, both opened from `@apackdev/ears/lmdb`, each with an engine of its own; packs and pack tests never load elmdb:

| Database | Directory | Holds | Opened by |
|---|---|---|---|
| The app's | `ears-db/` | Every entity and relation, held to the schema the registered packs declare | `openDatabaseStore` (`@apackdev/host/database`); the engine reads and writes it directly, keeping no copy in memory |
| The run history's | `run-history/` | Every flow run's nodes, as `RunNode` entities: each node a run made, with what it was given and returned | `openRunHistory`; `services.runHistory` reads and writes it through its own engine |

A flow run is not in the app's database: no unit (`transact`) on the app's engine reaches one, so a run's record is never undone by a unit that throws and never waits on one. As the run history opens it marks what the last session left running as `stopped`, and removes every session that ended more than 30 days ago, with everything it ran.
documents.name: architecture / Architecture / Persistence

documents.body:
## Backups

`@apackdev/host/backup`, reached by packs through `services.appData` (`@apackdev/host/services/app-data.ts`):

- **Export** (`exportBackup(targetPath, name?, databases?)`): copies the chosen stores (`lmdb`, the database, and `runHistory`; default `lmdb`) into `<targetPath>/<name>` (default `apack-backup-<timestamp>`), with a `metadata.json` and, when `lmdb` is included, `media/`.
- **Import** (`importBackup(path)`): requires `metadata.json`; restores only databases the app has. It copies the current files aside, closes the stores, replaces their files and media, reopens them and reloads memory; a restored run history's running nodes are marked `stopped`. On failure the previous files are put back and reloaded.
- **Reset** (`reset()`): clears the engine's memory, deletes the database and the run history and reopens them, clears the stored API keys, then runs `onInit`, app-line migrations, pack-line migrations and content application in dependency order, leaving the app as a fresh boot does.
documents.name: architecture / Architecture / Backups

documents.body:
## Generated files

`generate-entries` reads `apack.json` and produces modules and metadata in `src/__generated__/`, including files per dependency. Builds regenerate these when their declared inputs change; never edit them. The main outputs are listed below; some exist only when their contribution is declared.

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `pack-entry.ts` | BE registration: systems, services, repositories, steps, artifacts, blocks, EARS, lifecycle hooks, migrations, content writers, appliers, commands, features |
| `pack-entry-fe.ts` | FE registration: surfaces keyed by feature (the host registers each at its address), the default surface and designations by feature, step/artifact/block FE, settings forms, tiptap and app extensions. DSL definitions are discoverable snapshot data |
| `ears.ts` | Typed EARS namespace (Entity, RelKind constants + types), `PackShapes`, and the typed `query`/`find*`/`newId` facade |
| `ref.ts` | `ref(name)`: the ref (`<packId>/<featureId>`) a name in this pack's code stands for, its own features by id and any other by ref, bound to the pack so its code never passes its own pack id |
| `fe.ts` | `openSurface(name, event?)`, taking the names pack code writes, and the `SurfaceName` type, which lists exactly those names (the pack's own surfaces by feature id, its dependencies' by `<packId>/<featureId>`). Only packs with surfaces get it |
| `system-specs.ts` | Type-only: `specs`, the events each system receives and sends, keyed by feature id, read from its entry's spec. `events.ts` imports it; only packs with systems get it |
| `events.ts` | `SendableSurfaceEvents` (surface ID -> the events it receives: its own feature's system's, plus the inbox that surface's `Contract` declares), `PackSystemEvents`, and the typed `broadcastToSurface` (backend, every window), `sendToSurface` (renderer, this window) and `sendToSystem` |
| `types.ts` | Type barrel: each feature's `types` and step node types |
| `entity-destinations.json` / `event-contracts.json` | Build-checked entity destinations and event contracts, readable without executing pack modules |
| `settings.ts` / `settings-fe.ts` | Typed, owner-bound settings handles and frontend settings binding |
| `paths.ts` | `getDataDirPath(name)` for a directory in this pack's data namespace |
| `runtime-services.ts` | Shared runtime service binding used by the generated facade and registration |
| `services.ts` | Service aggregation: imports each service object its manifest entry names (`"path#exportName"`), exports `Services`/`Z`/`EntityId` and the host-selected `services` facade and `servicesForAction(label)` factory. `Services` types `services.emitter` as `PackEmitter`, with this pack's surface and system events |
| `repository.ts` | `repository`, typed with the repositories declared in `features.<id>.repositories` and dependencies' |
| `repositories.ts` | This pack's repositories by name, which `pack-entry.ts` puts in the registration (the app holds them with the pack's other contributions) |
| `pack-types.ts` | The facade types `apack pack build` bundles into `dist/types/pack-types.d.ts` for dependents |
| `deps/<id>.d.ts` | Each dependency's facade types, from its snapshot. Its header names the version (`// <id>@<version> facade types`); `apack pack build` warns when the dependency it builds with is another version |
| `deps/<id>.flow-helpers.js`, `.d.ts` | Each dependency's flow helpers module and declarations, from its snapshot |
| `references.ts` | Executable reference provider and icon bindings; identities and presentation metadata remain discoverable catalog data |
| `appliers.ts` | `appliers`, one per content key, which `pack-entry.ts` puts in the registration, and the compiled data path accessors (`setCompiledDir`, `getCompiledDir`) |
| `content-runtime.ts` | The pack's content runtime (entity types, relation kinds, repositories, content writers). The pack's tests import it; `apack pack build` bundles it into `dist/build/content-runtime.mjs` for dependents' tests |
| `flow-helpers.ts` | Typed DSL helpers for each step definition, with dependencies' |
| `step-types.ts` | Re-exports DSL/compiled node types from step definitions |

## FE build pipeline

The FE bundler uses Vite with `@vitejs/plugin-vue`:

- **Format:** ESM
- **Target:** es2022
- **Sourcemaps:** on, off with `--release`
- **Minification:** off, on with `--release`
- **Entry:** `src/pack-entry-fe.ts` (or `.js`) if present, otherwise `src/__generated__/pack-entry-fe.ts`
- **Output:** `dist/runtime/fe.js` + `dist/runtime/fe.css`
- `--skip-fe` skips it for packs without declared frontend bindings; a pack that declares them cannot publish a build without `runtime/fe.js`.

Pack builds run frontend compilation through the same captured file and namespace reads as earlier
phases. Final checks refuse publication when inputs no longer match the captured view, preserving the
accepted output.

Vue SFCs (`.vue` files) are compiled automatically — no extra build step needed.

## Build-time dependency resolution

`apack pack generate-entries`, `apack pack validate`, `apack pack build` and `apack pack fetch-deps` resolve each dependency in `apack.json` to its build output: `types/snapshot.json`, plus `build/` and `runtime/index.cjs` with its compiled content when it ships them (dependents' tests load the runtime). Sources, in order:

A selected host supplies its own packs before workspace lookup. An incompatible or unbuilt dependency belonging to that host fails; it never falls through to another app. Explicit `file:` dependencies override this selection. Without a host dependency, lookup continues in this order:

1. **`file:` path** — the given directory (relative to the pack root or absolute), in any layout. Not cached. A missing snapshot is an error.
2. **Workspace** — `../<id>`, `../../packages/<id>`, `../../<id>`.
3. **The app the pack is built against** — the built-in packs of a named app (`APACK_HOST`, `APACK_HOST_ROOT`) or of the apack checkout behind the pack.
4. **Installed apps** — `packs/<id>` in each environment's data dir (production, beta, development, test), which is where every pack that app has is installed, the ones it ships included.
5. **Cache** — `.apack/deps/<id>/`, used only when no source on this machine matches and the cached version satisfies the range. `fetch-deps` skips it.
6. **GitHub releases** — for `github:owner/repo [range]` values: the newest release matching the range, whose `<id>-<version>.tgz` is downloaded with its `.sha256`, checksum-checked, extracted and verified.
7. **Registry** — a stub for future `api.apack.dev` resolution. Currently a no-op.

Sources 2–4 must satisfy the declared semver range. Dependency type inspection validates the current
snapshot data contract and checks the facade exports codegen actually consumes. Recorded snapshot/SDK
stamps remain diagnostic context; absent or differing snapshot stamps do not invent a matching stamp
or authorize executable code. Cache entries retain that context. Only a matching snapshot format can
expose dependency build/runtime files. Type-only builds can proceed without those files; content
compilation and the test runtime refuse incompatible dependency execution before importing it.
A dependency found on this machine or on GitHub is cached under `.apack/deps/<id>/`
(`snapshot.json`, `facades/`, and eligible `build/`/`runtime/` files).

A `PackSnapshot` contains `format` (the snapshot format the writing CLI used), `types` (entity and relKind maps), `facades` (dependent-facing `.d.ts` contents, including the bundled `pack-types` facade), `entityDestinations` (entity wire name to local destination feature, compiled from surface `Contract.opens`), `manifest`, `sdkVersion`, `provenance` (which pack in its tree declares each name) and `flowHelpers` (the pack's bundled flow helpers module and declarations). Runtime/install readers use `PackSnapshot` with an exact execution stamp. Type-data readers use `PackDependencySnapshot`, retaining an optional recorded stamp and validating the same current fields; they do not read or convert another grammar.

Surface catalog entries project compiled destination claims as `opens`; unbuilt authoring previews do
not claim compiled destinations. Enabled native/installed claims must be unique per entity type, while
disabled claims remain visible. Native composition supplies `entityDestinations` as data and its accepted
frontend retains those claims; installed frontend eligibility uses the matching sealed build revision.
Catalog candidate validation runs before executable imports, enablement persistence and publication.

The common host/window catalog also exposes artifact and block declarations, including their owner,
origin, enablement and available declaration/build revisions. Artifact icons, block input kinds and
module references remain data when a pack is disabled or its implementation is unavailable. Reading
these declarations imports no viewer or backend module; executable registrations have a separate lifetime.


Step discovery reads `PackCatalogView.steps()`, whose entries carry the declaring pack, wire type,
origin and available declaration/build identity. Disabled installed and unbuilt source declarations remain
visible; executable component/layout readiness is separate. Active packs cannot share a step wire.
Native host composition uses the same step declaration grammar. Step defaults and presentation data
are captured at admission, so changing an authored object later does not mutate the accepted binding.

### Pack view failures

A failing pack canvas, panel, chat view or custom settings form shows an error in its own pane, with
its owner named. Other panes and host settings remain available. Retry remounts the current accepted
frontend; an unloaded or superseded version cannot be revived. A replacement resets its own failed
view, including when it reuses the same component. Settings declarations, defaults and saved values
remain intact; general settings and its JSON editor remain available after a custom form fails.
Contained errors are recorded with their pack and area without becoming window-fatal errors. The
native shell and settings runtime retain their host error handling. This contains Vue component
failures; it does not isolate arbitrary JavaScript or change pack permissions.

# CLI Reference

The `apack` CLI manages the desktop app and packs. Installed-app operations are root commands, app development uses repository npm scripts, and pack operations live under `apack pack`. Bare namespaces display help.

Pack operations cover scaffolding, code generation, building, validation, testing, releasing and installation. It also reads and repairs the app's database (`apack db`).

The npm CLI requires Node 22.15+ on the 22.x line, or Node 23.5+. The app-bundled CLI uses the app's included runtime.

documents.body:
### App operations and reports

`apack status [--channel production|beta|preview] [--json]` reports the installed app version, paths, and whether its default data profile is in use, without launching it. For running apps on custom profiles, use `apack profiles`.

`apack logs [--channel production|beta|preview] [--follow] [--lines <count>]` reads the installed app’s `main.log` (100 recent lines by default). Following waits for the file and follows rotation; Ctrl-C stops the reader.

`apack db backup --out <new-directory> [--profile <name> | --data-dir <path>]` creates a full backup compatible with `apack db import`. Close the app first. The database, the run history and media are included; installed packs and secrets are excluded. The backup directory is accessible only to its owner. Existing destinations and destinations inside the source data directory are refused.

`apack db backup verify <directory> [--json]` checks that each listed store opens and that the listed media is there, before restoration. It does not open your app data. It checks the backup format and completeness; entity-type compatibility depends on the packs installed when you import. Invalid backups exit nonzero; JSON reports include `valid: false` and the error.

`apack db recover --data-dir <profile> [--json]` lists interrupted import sessions; it only reads their recovery
records. To restore a selected session’s retained incumbent database, history and media, quit the app and run
`apack db recover --data-dir <profile> --session <reported-name> --restore`. A named `--profile` also works.
Close other tools reading the profile too. The command takes the profile’s offline write lock and reader exclusion,
validates the retained copies before changing live stores,
and retains the interrupted live files and incumbent copies inside the session. It resumes interrupted recovery;
a completed session is never restored again, even if the app has since written new data. Writable startup stays
blocked until recovery completes. Keep retained copies until you have verified your data; do not delete a pending
recovery record to bypass the block. SQLite candidate profiles additionally require `APACK_STORAGE_FORMAT=sqlite/1`
and must remain isolated from default profiles. Recovery requires readable intact incumbent copies and sufficient
space for a staged copy; malformed records, symlinks/special files or a changed staged copy refuse before publication.
Read-only profile tools register short-lived claims in private profile metadata so directory replacement cannot
race an open connection; profile metadata must be writable even though database contents remain read-only.
The backend’s direct read-only snapshot API is unchanged. Directory durability depends on the host/filesystem;
this command is not a universal power-loss guarantee.


The SQLite candidate also supports lossless database-only archives. Set `APACK_STORAGE_FORMAT=sqlite/1`
and name an isolated profile explicitly. `apack db dump --data-dir <profile> --primary <new-file>` writes
one primary archive; add `--runs <new-file>` for a separate history archive, or name only `--runs`.
Quit the app first. Output parents must exist, each target must be new and outside the source profile,
and a selected history store must already exist. Each completed file is an independent verified snapshot;
if a later export fails, completed files are retained and named. These archives preserve typed/raw values,
relations, counters and reusable embeddings; `db export` JSON/CSV remains a display format.

`apack db load --data-dir <profile> --primary <file> [--runs <file>]` fully verifies, rebuilds, audits and
checks the selected archives against the installed settings contract without replacing data. It uses
private staging space and may take substantial disk/time; memory can scale with the largest individual
value. Add `--force` to replace the selected stores through the protected import/recovery path. A history-only
load leaves primary data and its commit unchanged. Every selected input validates before replacement;
unknown outcomes retain incumbent recovery copies for `db recover`. Media, packs and secrets are not part
of these files, and current media is preserved. Use `db backup` for a full database-and-media backup.
Archive publication requires hard-link support; unsupported filesystems refuse. Directory durability and
Windows inherited permissions depend on the host/filesystem; this is not a universal power-loss guarantee.
A killed export can leave a private `.apack-logical-export-*` directory beside its output. Stop exporting
tools and verify any retained output before removing such scratch directories; retry does not delete them.

`apack pack outdated [--profile <name>] [--json]` checks GitHub-installed packs for newer releases compatible with the profile’s recorded app version. Beta profiles include prereleases. Local/URL installs and app-shipped packs are reported as unmanaged. A failed check exits nonzero; finding an update alone does not. CLI GitHub installs record their source for subsequent checks; uninstall removes that record.

`apack pack upgrade <id> [--profile <name>]` upgrades a GitHub-installed pack to its newest compatible release. Close the app first. The recorded app version and pack format are required. Checksums, pack identity/version, host compatibility, build format, enabled dependencies, and installed packs that depend on it are checked before replacement. Local/URL installs and app-managed packs are not upgraded by this command. A user-managed fork at an app-default ID can use its recorded GitHub source.

`apack doctor --json` emits one object with `channel`, `healthy`, and individual `checks`. Failed checks remain in the JSON report and the command exits nonzero.

`apack profiles --json [--all] [--sizes]` emits `environments` and `profiles` arrays, including their paths and running state. Temporary profiles require `--all`; numeric byte sizes require `--sizes`. JSON is supported for listings only.

`apack pack list --json [--profile <name>]` emits one object containing the selected profile, packs directory, and installed packs with their identity, version, enabled state, dependencies, and recorded update source. Unreadable manifests or installation records fail explicitly.

Reporting commands emit one JSON object on stdout when `--json` is selected. Errors go to stderr and exit nonzero. Human-readable output remains the default.

### Scaffolding

#### `apack pack init [name]`

Create a new pack from scratch. `name` is the pack id: lowercase letters, digits and hyphens (prompted for when omitted). The directory must not exist.

```bash
apack pack init my-pack
```

Creates no feature (add one with `apack pack add feature`). It writes:

- `apack.json`: one entity type named after the pack, empty `features`, `dependencies` and `permissions`, and `content.sources` with `actions`, `flows` and an `examples` entry using the `examples` content format (`markdown-tree`). No `extensions` section: `apack pack add step|artifact|block` each declare their own entry under it
- `package.json` (depends on `@apackdev/sdk`; pins `@apackdev/cli`, `@apackdev/testing`, `vitest`, `typescript`), `tsconfig.json`, `.gitignore`, `src/env.d.ts`
- `.github/workflows/release.yml`: publishes the GitHub release when `apack pack release` pushes a `v*` tag
- `src/content/actions/`, `src/content/flows/`, `src/content/examples/hello.md`
- `vitest.config.ts`, `tests/setup.ts` (the `@apackdev/testing/harness` setup) and `tests/<name>.spec.ts`

Then runs `generate` and `generate-entries`.

#### `apack pack add <entity> <name> [options]`

Add an entity to an existing pack. Run from inside a pack directory. Names other than a feature's are kebab-case (`^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$`). Existing files are never overwritten.

| Entity | Command | What it creates |
|---|---|---|
| Feature | `apack pack add feature <name> --description <purpose> [--label <Label>] [--icon <Icon>] [--designation <role>]` | See below |
| Step | `apack pack add step <type> [--trigger]` | `src/extensions/steps/<type>/{build.ts,types.ts,form.vue}` (`types.ts` declares `DSL<Type>Node` and `<Type>Node`); with `--trigger`, `trigger.ts` in place of `build.ts`, holding a `TriggerFacet` rather than a `StepBuildFacet`. Declares one `extensions.steps.<type>` entry with inline `node` labels/defaults, an explicit `types` module, a `build` or `trigger` binding, and inline `fe` presentation with a lazy form target |
| Artifact | `apack pack add artifact <type> [--icon <Icon>]` | `src/extensions/artifacts/viewers/<type>-artifact.vue`; when the manifest declares `artifacts`, adds `{ type, fe: { icon } }` to that register file and the viewer to its `-fe.ts` `componentMap` |
| Block | `apack pack add block <type> [--input]` | `src/extensions/blocks/display/<Type>Block.vue` (or `input/<Type>Input.vue`); updates the `blocks` register file and its `-fe.ts` when the manifest declares `blocks` |
| Action | `apack pack add action <name> [--category <cat>]` | `src/content/actions/<category>/<name>.ts` (category defaults to the pack id) |
| Prompt | `apack pack add prompt <name>` | `src/content/prompts/<name>.ts` |
| Flow | `apack pack add flow <name>` | `src/content/flows/<name>.ts`. Needs a dependency that provides flow steps (e.g. `default-setup`) |
| Command | `apack pack add command <name> [--placeholder <text>] [--document <name>] [--folder <name>]` | A chat slash command: one `**<name>**: <placeholder>` line in a document under the `commands` source. A command is a line rather than a document, so one named with `--document` that already exists gains the line in its field section — several commands take no markdown editing in between. Refuses a name that document already defines, and a document with no field section |
| Document | `apack pack add document <name> [--content <text>] [--section <type>] [--folder <name>] [--tag <tag>]` | A document under the `documents` source. `--content` is the body, written as given — so a caller that already has the text needs no second step, and content holding its own `<!-- section:… -->` markers writes several sections. Without it the body explains the convention instead |
| Service | `apack pack add service <name> [--feature <feature>]` | `src/extensions/services/<name>.ts` in `extensions.services`, or `src/features/<feature>/be/services/<name>.ts` in that feature's `services`. The key is the camelCased name, the value `path#<camelName>Service` |
| Migration | `apack pack add migration [version] [--version <ver>]` | `src/migrations/<version>.ts` exporting `up()`, with a declarative description and function reference under `migrations.pack` (or `migrations.app` with `--app`). Version defaults to the manifest's |

`add feature`, `add service`, `add step`, `add artifact` and `add block` each declare what they add in `apack.json` and then run `generate-entries`, because the manifest entry is the whole declaration and codegen is what carries it into the pack's entries — there is no barrel to edit. `add migration` declares its own entry too. `add action`, `add prompt` and `add flow` only write files, their content being found by the directory `content.sources` already names. `add command` and `add document` are between the two: each writes a markdown document and declares the SDK's `commands` or `documents` source for it when the pack has none, so they need no format and no dependency. `--folder` nests it, which the compiler reads as the collection holding it. In a pack whose dependencies aren't installed yet, `generate-entries` can't read a system's events through `@apackdev/sdk`: the files and `apack.json` are still written, and `npm install` regenerates the entries (the pack's `prepare` script).

**`add feature`.** The name is the feature id: a lowercase letter, then letters and digits (`notes`, `calendarEvents`), because it becomes an identifier in generated code. `--designation`, if given, names the role it plays and may differ from the feature id. It creates:

- `src/features/<name>/be/system.ts`, `be/contract.ts` (the system's contract, which `apack.json` names), `be/types.ts`, `be/repository/index.ts`
- `src/features/<name>/fe/state.ts`, `fe/contract.ts`, `fe/canvas/list.vue`, `fe/settings.vue`
- `tests/features/<name>/be/system.spec.ts` (and `tests/setup.ts` with its devDependencies if the pack has none)

and adds a keyed `features.<name>` entry with its required `description`, explicit `types` pointing at `be/types.ts`, `settings` (including the custom `form` it writes), `system.entry`, `surface` (`state`, `canvas`, `label`, `icon`), empty `services`, and `repositories` `<name>Queries` and `<name>Commands` pointing at `be/repository/index.ts`.

### Code generation

#### `apack pack generate-entries`

Read `apack.json` and generate all files in `src/__generated__/`. Uses input hashing to skip when the manifest and template haven't changed. Pass `--force` to regenerate unconditionally.

#### `apack pack fetch-deps`

Resolve every dependency into `.apack/deps/<id>/`: a resolution record retains the declared spec, exact version, origin and content revision; immutable builds retain the complete verified pack layout. Resolution order:

1. Explicit `file:` dependencies: read directly, with no fallback
2. A selected host's own dependency builds, when `APACK_HOST` or the CLI's resolved host handoff is present
3. The workspace: nearest ancestor first, `packages/<id>` then `<id>`
4. The linked checkout when no host was explicitly selected
5. Installed app packs, then cached builds or GitHub releases as applicable

Every source must satisfy the declared range and pack identity. Current type data can be inspected independently of its executable-format stamp. Executable files require a matching stamp and a verified complete build; type-only data exposes no executable paths. A selected host's unbuilt or
incompatible dependency fails rather than being replaced by another workspace or app. Explicit
`file:` dependencies remain authoritative and are copied into a verified cache build for builds and tests. A cache hit preserves its original provenance; changed GitHub origins cannot reuse another repository’s cached resolution. Publication keeps previously resolved build paths intact. `apack pack build` uses the same resolution rules;
see [Manifest Reference — Dependencies](manifest.md#dependencies).

documents.body:
### Building

#### `apack pack build [--skip-generate] [--skip-fe] [--release]`

A build writes a verified pack layout into a staging directory, then replaces `dist/` only after
all phases succeed. A failed build preserves the previous complete `dist/`. See
[pack builds](pack-builds.md) for the build, archive, installed and native layouts.

The build:

1. Validates `apack.json`, prepares staging, and resolves dependencies.
2. Generates `src/__generated__/` from declarations and dependency snapshots (`--skip-generate` requires unchanged generation inputs and exact recorded output bytes; stale or missing files refuse before bundling). Declared settings schemas/defaults are inline; custom forms are separate declared modules.
3. Enforces pack rules, including the manifest's `checks.allow`, and refuses unresolved dependencies. Warns if generated dependency types differ from the resolved versions.
4. Compiles `content.sources` into `runtime/content/`, validating flows against dependency step build code, and bundles declared content compilers for dependents.
5. Bundles and checks the standalone `types/pack-types.d.ts` facade. Its imports must resolve through `@apackdev/*`, SDK peers or Node built-ins; a committed facade report mismatch produces a warning (`apack pack facade-report`).
6. Bundles flow helpers, step build facets and the content runtime used by dependents. Checks that the content runtime can load in a fresh Node process with the supported SDK dependencies.
7. Builds declared Monaco DSL definitions, the backend runtime, and the frontend unless `--skip-fe`. The frontend entry is `src/pack-entry-fe.ts` (or `.js`) when present, otherwise the generated entry. `--skip-fe` is valid only for packs with no declared frontend bindings: surfaces, designations, reference providers, custom settings forms, steps, artifacts, blocks, text editor extensions or app extensions require the frontend entry. An incomplete build refuses publication and retains the existing `dist/`.
8. Validates the snapshot and generated declaration identities, refuses inputs changed during the build, writes the manifest and integrity receipt, verifies the completed layout, and publishes staging as `dist/`.

The snapshot includes declaration data, entity/relation types, facade declarations, compiled help,
flow helpers and contribution provenance. Explicit `null` entity shapes remain untyped. Build-time
compilers, helpers and content runtime may execute during building; inspecting the completed snapshot
does not execute them. Discovery and executable bindings are separate contracts.

Compiled content has a separate verified `runtime/content/content.json` index. The common build reader
checks its owner, exact compiled source/dataset membership, written policy and required data files;
`apack pack info` uses that captured inventory. An omitted index or data file fails validation even
when an incomplete producer sealed the remaining files successfully.

Bundle and gate failures are reported and exit with code 1. `--release` minifies and drops source maps.
Files under `public/` are copied into the frontend output from the build's captured authored inputs.

Compiler workers inherit Node options from `NODE_OPTIONS`, including ordered `--require` and `--import`
preloads. Node arguments passed directly to the CLI configure its supervisor; custom export conditions
are also forwarded to the worker. Use `NODE_OPTIONS` when configuring compiler execution.
The separate published-content runtime check omits those options so compiler initialization cannot
hide missing runtime dependencies or provide globals that dependent packs will not have.
On macOS, native addon admission checks library dependencies and matching `DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH`
candidates. A library selected outside the captured package or normal OS libraries is refused before
addon initialization; an unused search directory is allowed.
`DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` executes before that module-loading boundary and accepts normal OS libraries.
Load package libraries through captured compiler modules rather than inserting live package paths.
`DYLD_VERSIONED_LIBRARY_PATH` and `DYLD_VERSIONED_FRAMEWORK_PATH` accept only absolute operating-system
directories under `/usr/lib` or `/System/Library`, including their physical targets. Other configured
directories are refused before worker launch, even if their entries might be unused. Unset these
variables and use captured package-relative dependencies for package libraries.
`DYLD_SHARED_CACHE_DIR` selects a single directory and follows the same OS-directory policy. The normal
OS shared cache remains supported; custom caches outside OS library locations are refused before launch.

On Linux, ELF admission checks declared dependencies before addon initialization. Package libraries
must resolve through captured `$ORIGIN` paths; absolute paths back to a source package are refused.
Search uses launch-time loader tokens, RPATH/RUNPATH, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, the OS library cache and
default directories. `LD_PRELOAD`, `LD_AUDIT` and system-wide preload entries accept normal OS library
paths only. The installed ELF interpreter supplies its own search metadata; no `readelf` or `ldd`
installation is required. Failure to obtain that metadata is explicit.
The runtime's own linked libraries are checked before launch using the child executable, environment
and working directory. An unused `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` directory is allowed; a selected outside runtime
library is refused before its initialization code can run.

`apack pack build --watch` watches authored inputs throughout the pack, including `apack.json`,
modules outside `src/`, JSON schemas, assets and help. The authored watcher excludes generated,
build, dependency and Git trees. Compiler configuration, resolved TypeScript files and unresolved
lookup candidates are watched separately, including outside the pack; repairing a missing target
can rebuild without another authored edit. Linked authored data is watched through atomic replacement and retargeting; executable
module references still must remain physically inside the pack. It publishes through the same staged
build in a fresh CLI process before requesting development-host reload, so changed flow, step and
compiler modules cannot reuse the previous build's module cache;
invalid edits retain the previous verified build. Saves during a build schedule another run.
`--watch` cannot be combined with other build flags. This builds the complete build and can take
longer than rebundling only the runtime. `apack pack dev` uses this watcher and installs each successful
publication before reloading; Vite continues serving frontend changes.

A build also writes `.apack/reads.json`: the files each bundling phase read, as esbuild, Rollup and Vite report them, keyed by phase and relative to the pack. It is the build's own record of its inputs — what a build system calls a dep file — for a cache or a CI check that wants to know whether what it declared covers what the build touched; the build never reads it back, and a phase that didn't run is absent rather than empty. `APACK_NO_BUILD_READS=1` turns it off, for a read-only tree.

Selected hosts supply their built-in pack dependencies before ambient workspace copies. Incompatible or unbuilt host dependencies fail; explicit manifest `file:` dependencies remain authoritative.

A build resolves the pack's `@apackdev` packages to the `dist` each published package ships — the one layout a pack ever has, whether the packages came from the registry or from a link to an apack checkout. There is nothing to configure, and a pack's own configs set no resolution conditions. `apack pack test` and `apack pack dev` resolve the same way, so a pack's tests run against what its build compiled; against a checkout they first bring that `dist` up to date with the checkout's sources.

#### `apack pack archive [--out <dir>]`

Verify the build-owned `dist/integrity.json` and stage its recorded files into a verified pack (`integrity.json` lists a sha256 per file) and write `<id>-<version>.tgz` and `<id>-<version>.tgz.sha256` to `--out` (default: `.apack/archives`). Run `apack pack build` first (`--release` for publishable output). Verifies sealed output and recorded source/dependency inputs under the build lock, using the selected build’s compiler/options context. Rechecks inputs before publishing the archive; changed inputs refuse without replacing the previous archive. Keep custom output under `.apack/` or outside the pack to avoid introducing generated files into authored inputs.

#### `apack pack dev`

Launch apack with your pack installed and keep it in step with your edits.

It picks an app the way you tell it to — `--host <path>` for a local apack checkout, `--host beta` for a Beta that satisfies your `hostVersion` (a downloaded one if you have it, the newest otherwise) — and **with neither it works one out rather than asking**: the apack checkout your pack is built against, if there is one, else a cached/downloaded compatible Beta. Nothing is remembered, nothing is asked, and it prints which app it chose and which rule chose it.

Deriving the checkout is the right pairing rather than a convenience: a pack whose `@apackdev/*` resolve into a checkout is *compiled against that checkout's packages*, so running it inside a released Beta would pair source-built pack code with a released host. If that checkout is not built, `dev` says so and names `npm run build:default-setup && npm run build:runtime` instead of quietly using a Beta you were not built against.

`apack pack test` deliberately derives nothing — it pins from your `hostVersion` — so a test run means the same thing on a fresh machine as on one you have been developing on.

The environment follows the app: a checkout runs as `development`, and a packaged Beta runs as `beta`, because a packaged build stamps its own channel. Neither touches production data.

**Profiles.** By default `dev` uses the shared development data dir, so every run inherits what the last one left. A profile is a data dir of its own, created on demand:

- `--profile <name>` — that one, created the first time you name it, and kept
- `--fresh` — a new one, whose name is printed so you can come back to it with `--profile`
- `--fresh --rm` — the same, removed when the command exits
- `--profile <name> --rm` — the same for a name you choose. It removes only a profile **this run creates**: one that is already there holds data you kept, so the flag is refused rather than quietly ignored, and `apack profiles rm <name>` is what removes that one
- `--with-secrets` — copy the secrets this environment already holds into the **new** profile, so a throwaway run can use them without you entering anything again. The values are encrypted in the profile's own data dir, and the data key that decrypts them goes in a file beside them rather than the OS credential store, so `rm -rf` removes both; that also means they are protected by file permissions alone, which is the trade every profile makes and which Settings states

A profile is self-contained — its data, packs, logs and secrets are all inside it, and the data key that encrypts its secrets goes in a file beside them rather than into the OS keychain, which is shared by every app of one channel. So `rm -rf` is the whole cleanup, and `apack profiles rm <name>` does it for you. The path is printed, and `apack db --profile <name>` opens its database — by the same name `dev` and `profiles` show, throwaway ones included.

A profile is a data dir and nothing else: the environment, the app's identity and the URL scheme are untouched, so `--host beta` and a local checkout can both run the same profile. **The word is `profile` rather than `instance` because an instance of an app is a running process** — which is what Electron's single-instance lock is about — where this is storage, and a named, disposable data dir that leaves the app's identity alone is what a browser calls a profile.

`dev` first builds the pack, then starts or reuses the app on that data dir and installs the verified
build. Closing `dev` closes the app it started. It then:

- serves the FE entry from a Vite dev server (port 5199, or the next free one) with HMR, recording its port in `pack-dev-servers/<id>.json` in the app's data dir so the app's `pack://` requests go to it. The marker sits outside the installed pack, which stays exactly the verified files, and is removed when `apack pack dev` exits
- on `apack.json` changes, regenerates `src/__generated__/`
- on authored input changes, rebuilds and has the app install the verified pack. A checkout's app installs and starts each build itself. A packaged app (`--host beta`) cannot be asked to, so `dev` copies the build in while the app is stopped: a rebuild that changes the backend restarts the app `dev` started, and one that changes only the frontend leaves it to Vite

Backend builds and Vite use the same captured compiler generation. A compiler refresh starts a ready
replacement server, updates its marker and retires the old server; a failed replacement startup keeps
the incumbent. Each server owns its writable cache. Packs without an FE entry use the same build watcher.
Development configuration changes replace the server with the next successful build; ordinary source
edits continue through HMR.

#### `apack pack drive [script | --eval <body>] [--host <path>] [profile flags]`

Launch apack and drive it from a script: navigate, send events, read state, take screenshots.

**This is mainly for an agent.** It is how a coding agent debugs and develops against the app it is changing — open the thing it just built, click through it, read the state back, screenshot it, and see for itself whether the change worked. A person can use it the same way, and the app's windows are shown so you can watch, but the reason it exists is that an agent has no other way to look at a running app.

**It is not testing, and nothing treats it as testing.** A driving script asserts nothing, nothing gates on it, and no test runner collects it. Scripts live in `drive/`, which `apack pack drive` creates the first time you run it, and which sits outside every test glob by construction rather than by exclusion. `apack pack test` never sees it.

```ts
// drive/notes.ts
import { drive } from '@apackdev/testing';

drive('open notes and look at it', async ({ app, appPage }) => {
  await app.navigate('notes');
  await app.screenshot('notes');
  // appPage is a Playwright Page: click, type, evaluate — whatever you need
});
```

The import is `drive`, not `test`: the same runner under a name that says what the file is. With no script argument every file in `drive/` runs; name one to run just it.

##### One question, many times

A driving script is a closed program. It runs, it ends, and the next question costs another edit and
another app launch. So a question is asked of the app `apack pack dev` is already holding, over the debug port
that app published — one process per question, no session to stand up and nothing to tear down.

```bash
apack pack dev                                   # one terminal: holds the app
apack pack drive --state                         # another: 0.9s
apack pack drive --eval 'return window.appVersion'
apack pack drive --query 'return query(EARS.Entity.Note).count()'
```

With no app running it exits 3 and says so. `--spawn` starts one and keeps it, so a cold checkout costs
one flag on the first question and an attach on every one after.

**Three rules, so a verb is guessable.** A POST is a verb and a GET is a noun; one concept has one field
name, in requests and in responses (`code` is any source the session runs, `surface` names a surface
whichever direction it travels); and every answer is `{ ok, value }`, or `{ ok: false, error }` when the
operation failed — a `4xx` means nothing ran at all.

| verb | method | body | does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/eval` | POST | `{ code }` | runs the code in the window and returns what it returns |
| `/send` | POST | `{ event, to? }` | sends an event to a system by ref, or to the app's root actor without `to` |
| `/query` | POST | `{ code }` | runs query code against the live database |
| `/transact` | POST | `{ code }` | runs transaction code against the live database |
| `/state` | GET | — | the state value, the active `surface` and the `surfaces` list |
| `/wait` | POST | `{ state }` or `{ surface }`, `{ timeoutMs }` | waits for a dotted state path, or for a surface to arrive |
| `/navigate` | POST | `{ surface }` | opens a surface |
| `/surface` | POST | `{ surface, path? }` | what that surface published, or one dotted path into it |
| `/click` | POST | `{ selector }` | clicks what it matches |
| `/fill` | POST | `{ selector, text }` | types into it |
| `/press` | POST | `{ key, selector? }` | a key, to an element or to the page |
| `/snapshot` | GET | — | the page as an accessibility tree |
| `/logs` | POST | `{ since?, source? }` | the app's own log, after a line you saw and from one source |
| `/settings` | GET | — | host settings snapshot: effective values, status and catalog metadata |
| `/viewport` | GET | — | the size the app is rendering into |
| `/set-viewport` | POST | `{ width, height }` | changes it |
| `/set-setting` | POST | `{ target, path, value }` | writes one setting |
| `/screenshot` | POST | `{ name }` | writes `.apack/drive/screenshots/<name>.png` |
| `/reload` | POST | — | reloads the window and returns once it is connected again |
| `/events` | POST | — | the app's events since you last asked, and how many were dropped |
| `/drops` | POST | — | sends the bus dropped, and clears them |
| `/errors` | POST | — | renderer errors, and clears them |
| `/close` | POST | — | ends the session and shuts the app down |

**`/snapshot` is usually what you want over `/screenshot`.** It answers with the page as text: readable,
diffable, cheap, and it says what a thing *is* rather than where it is. `/screenshot` is for a person
looking at the result afterwards.

**`/settings` answers with the *stored* document**, not the effective one: it is what a write lands in, so
it is what says whether your write landed. The defaults come from the host for app preferences and pack declarations for contributed values.

**A refused write answers `ok: false`, with the reasons.** The settings store checks the whole next
document and refuses what it will not take — an unknown feature ref, an undeclared pack group, a change
while a backup is being imported — and `/set-setting` waits for that answer rather than for the send to be
accepted. It used to resolve on the send, so every refusal read as success.

**`/set-setting` uses an explicit settings owner.** Set `target` to `{"kind":"app"}`,
`{"kind":"feature","featureRef":"default-setup/code"}`, or
`{"kind":"pack","packId":"default-setup","groupId":"assistant"}`. `path` is a dotted string
relative to that owner, such as `personal.name` for app settings or `name` for the assistant group.
The writer validates the value and reports refusals. `/settings` reads the host's current snapshot,
including composed defaults and stored choices, rather than reading the sparse database row directly.

**`/set-viewport` resizes whichever thing the run actually has.** A session whose window is shown — a
person watching `apack pack drive` — has its *window* resized, because a viewport Playwright sets is an
emulation inside the window: the app would draw into one corner and leave the desktop showing through the
rest. A session nobody is watching gets that emulation, which is what makes a suite's layout the same
everywhere. Either way `/viewport` answers with what the layout has, read from the window.

**`/surface` over `/eval`.** A surface's state is what its view is showing, so reading it is the commonest
question there is; doing it through `/eval` means writing the same expression, with the same ref and the
same optional chain, every time.

The three drains are POSTs because each one *clears* what it returns: draining is right for a session open
for an hour, but a GET that answers differently on a retry is a trap.

**A write does not update the UI; `/reload` is how you see it.** A surface's state is what its system
sent it, so a write made outside that system — `/transact`, the database console, `apack db exec` — changes
the database and reaches no view. That is the console being a console rather than a fault, and it is not
staleness that time fixes: navigating between surfaces does not refresh one, because the surface's actor
survives. `/reload` does, because a new connection makes every system send its startup data again.

`window.location.reload()` from `/eval` is not an alternative. The app blocks renderer-initiated
navigation, so it returns having done nothing — which reads exactly like a reload that changed nothing.

**`/wait` rather than re-asking `/state`.** `{"state":"running.connected"}` returns when the app gets
there; `{"surface":"default-setup/notes"}` returns when that surface registers. One of the two, never both.

**Replies come to the session, and each names the request it answers.** Both matter. The session has its
own connection to the app and a name on it, so an answer is addressed here rather than to every window —
a person querying in the Database surface while you drive is no longer mistaken for you. And because three
concurrent `/query` calls would otherwise be indistinguishable, each reply still names its request, so they
may run together and one you stopped waiting for is ignored.

**`/query` and `/transact` reach the live database**, not the files on disk — they go to the running app, so a
write is visible to the next read in the same session. `apack db exec` cannot do that: it refuses while
the app holds the write lock.

**A failed verb answers `200` with `{ "ok": false, "error": ... }`** — the request was fine and the
operation was not, which is the common case while driving. A malformed request, a missing token or an
unknown verb answers `4xx`, because nothing ran.

The app's own output is in `.apack/drive/results/app-0.log` for the whole session, so there is nothing to stream.

##### One question

A script and a session both assume you have more than one question. For the first one — and often the only
one — `--eval`, `--query` and `--state` attach to a development app, ask one thing, print it and exit. Without a session they exit 3; `--spawn` explicitly starts one:

```bash
apack pack drive --eval 'return document.title'
{"value":"Agent X","state":"attached","startedBy":"dev","supervisorPid":12345}
```

The answer is one object with `value`, `state`, `startedBy` and `supervisorPid`, as **one JSON line on stdout and
nothing else there**, so `$(apack pack drive --eval …)` is directly parseable; the app's output goes to stderr
and the exit code is the status. It runs headless, since nothing is watching a single question.

`--eval` takes a function **body**, not an expression, so `return` is required and a body without one
answers no value at all.

**`apack pack drive` requires a pack** and installs it into the isolated app used by a script.

Scripts select an executable with `--host <path>`; pack scripts also accept `--host beta`. Live questions select a source development session with `--profile`. `--host` requires `--spawn`; an existing session must belong to that host. Fresh live questions require `--spawn`. The two modes have different ownership:

- **A question** joins the app `apack pack dev` is holding, over the debug port in that app's session file. It asks of the development data dir unless `--profile <name>` names another, because that is where the app you are working in is.
- **A script** launches its own app and shows its windows, in a fresh data dir thrown away afterwards, so a driving session starts clean and leaves nothing and a script's result does not depend on whatever surface the last one left open. `--profile <name>` is how a session keeps its state for the next one.

Electron allows one app per data dir, which is what makes a question *join* rather than compete — and why a script, which wants an app of its own, gets a dir of its own with it. If a person wants to watch what a script is doing they watch its window; a question is headless, since nothing is watching one question.

### Which app, and how long it lives

| What you run | The app it uses | When it closes |
|---|---|---|
| `apack pack dev` | starts its own | when you stop the command |
| `apack pack drive --eval` (and the other one-shots) | a live one; **fails if there is none** | it was not yours to close |
| the same, with `--spawn` | a live one, else it starts one | **it stays for the next question** — and, on a profile, closes itself after 10 minutes with nothing attached |
| `apack pack drive <script>` | always its own | when the script finishes |
| `apack pack test` | always its own, isolated | when the run finishes |

**A question keeps the app so the next question is cheap; a script closes it so its result does not depend
on what the last one left behind; and a question never starts one unless you asked.** That is the whole
rule. Measured on a checkout: `--spawn` and the first answer together, 3.3s; every question after it, 0.9s.

Only one app can run per data dir, which is why `drive` joins yours rather than competing with it, and why
`--profile <name>` is how you get a second one.

**A one-shot's stdout is one JSON object and nothing else**, so it pipes:

```
{"value":"0.3.14","state":"attached","startedBy":"dev","supervisorPid":75415}
```

`value` is the answer, `state` is `attached` or `spawned`, `startedBy` says whose app answered, and
`supervisorPid` is what ends it. The exit code is the status, and there are three: **0** with a value,
**3** when no app is running, **1** when the verb failed. Those last two are different answers — a miss is
worth retrying with `--spawn` and a failed verb is not — and neither puts anything on stdout, so a pipe
never receives half an answer.

A run that **started** an app says so on stderr and names the two ways to end it: `apack pack dev`, which takes
the directory back, or the `supervisorPid` above. An attach that changed nothing says nothing, because the
fields already said it.

**And nothing is left running forever.** Which of the two applies depends on where the app is, because the
two cases have different answers:

- **On your development data dir** — a `--spawn` with no profile flags — the app stays until you take the
  directory back, which `apack pack dev` and `npm run dev` do for you: they close the one a question started,
  say so, and start yours. So there is nothing to remember, and no timer closes an app you may be watching.
- **On a profile** — `--profile <name>` — nothing reclaims it that way, so the app closes itself after **10
  minutes** with no question attached. Each question resets that, so a session you are working in keeps
  its app; one you walked away from gives the data dir back. It tells you at launch, and says why in its
  log when it goes.

`apack profiles` lists every data dir with a live app, who started it, and the pid that ends it — which is
the answer when a terminal has been scrolled away and you want to know what is still up.

Live questions require `--spawn` for `--fresh`, `--rm`, or `--with-secrets`. Cleanup and secret-copy
flags require a new session and are refused when an existing session would be reused, including
when another caller wins the spawn race. `--with-secrets` refuses an existing profile.
