### Validation

#### `apack pack validate [--json]`

Read-only authoring checks. Exit codes are `0` for valid, `1` for invalid and `2` for incomplete
validation (for example, unresolved dependencies prevent codegen checks). An incomplete report names
the skipped checks and never claims the pack is valid. Build and installation remain strict gates.
`--json` prints one report with `status`, `diagnostics` and `skippedChecks`; diagnostics carry a stable
code, severity, manifest path, message and owner/source/suggestion when available. Text output renders
the same report.

Checks:
- Manifest structure validation
- Declared module files: feature types/contracts, systems, surfaces, references and forms; entity shapes; services, repositories, steps, blocks, artifacts, DSL modules, frontend extensions, lifecycle hooks, migrations and content writers/compilers/appliers. Paths stay within the pack, including symlinks. File checks run even when dependencies are unresolved.
- Feature designation ownership: no two features claim the same role
- Static export and contract checks through in-memory codegen when source files and dependencies are available; modules are not activated
- Dependency resolution (a warning when one can't be resolved)
- **What your pack's code may say** — the same rules `apack pack build` refuses on, reported here without building:

| Rule | What it refuses | Switchable? |
|---|---|---|
| `contract-leaves` | a contract that reaches its own machine (`./state.ts`, `./system.ts`), another feature, or generated code beyond `#generated/types` and `#generated/ears`. Codegen reads a contract as a declared type before it writes anything, so a contract whose read positions resolve through the machine collapses to `any` and the build fails for good — and one that resolves anyway ships the machine's whole declaration in your published facade | no |
| `source-resolution` | a `tsconfig.json` or Vitest config of yours that resolves a checkout's `@apackdev` source instead of the published `dist` — esbuild and the pack bundler read `dist` either way, so such a pack typechecks against one thing and ships another | no |
| `own-modules` | a specifier that names no file: `#generated/events` or `#generated/events.js` where the file is `events.ts`, and a relative `./x.js` whose source sibling is `./x.ts`. No runtime resolves an extensionless specifier in ESM, and a pack ships one bundle rather than a module per source | no |
| `pack-own-aliases` | `@/…`, a TypeScript-only `paths` mapping no runtime reads. Name your own modules with `#` subpath imports from your `package.json` | no |
| `internal-package-imports` | an `@apackdev` export named `_x`: it is `@internal`, the app's own, and an app update is free to rename it | no |
| `host-imports` | `@apackdev/host`, which is not installed for a pack | no |
| `database-imports` | Native database packages or app-only `@apackdev/ears/lmdb` and `/sqlite` entries: use the engine the app binds | no |
| `untyped-sends` | `untypedBroadcastToSurface`, `untypedSendToSystem` — use the typed facades from `#generated/events` | yes |
| `raw-transport` | `_rootEvents`, `trpc.bus`, `@apackdev/sdk/rpc` | yes |
| `backend-console` | `console.*` under `features/*/be/`, `migrations/` or `extensions/` — use `createLogger` from `@apackdev/sdk/logger` | yes |
| `component-sends` | `sendToSurface` from a feature's `.vue`. A component runs in no delivery, so the send carries no `Message.sender` and the surface it reaches cannot answer it — emit to your own surface with `useSurface()` and let its machine send. An extension's component is exempt: it is rendered in no surface scope and by no single surface, so it addresses a surface by ref and `sendToSurface` is that route's send | no |
| `cross-feature-imports` | a module of another feature's `fe/`, and a feature passing its own frontend on (`export … from './fe/state.ts'`). What a feature offers the rest is its surface's contract, read through `#generated/fe` and `#generated/events` | yes |
| `window-storage` | `localStorage` or `sessionStorage` anywhere in a pack — reach your surface's own storage through `surfaceStorage`/`useSurfaceStorage` from `@apackdev/sdk/fe`, which prefixes every name with the surface's ref. A window's storage is one flat namespace, so a hand-written key is one another pack can pick — which is why this one is not switchable: allowing it takes the collision out on somebody else | no |
| `repository-casts` | `repository as unknown as …`, reading a repository through a type its owner never declared. `repository` from `#generated/repository` is already typed with your own repositories and your dependencies' | yes |
| `reserved-event-keys` | a property named `_call`, in `src` or `tests`. That key is the app's: a delivery door writes the call a message answers under it, so a field of yours by that name is overwritten on the way in and read as a correlation on the way out. Ask `answersCall(event, outstanding)` or `settleCall(pending, event)` from `@apackdev/sdk/events` instead of reading it, build an answer in a test with `answerTo` from `@apackdev/sdk/testing`, and rename a field of your own that collides | no |

A rule marked switchable is a development convention a pack may allow in **`apack.json`**:

```json
{ "checks": { "allow": ["backend-console", "untyped-sends"] } }
```

The others report something that breaks — a specifier nothing resolves, an import the bundler refuses, a name
the next app version may rename — so there is nothing to allow, and naming one in `allow` is an error.

Exits with code 1 on errors.

#### `apack pack doctor [--json]`

Read-only source health using the same manifest, target, static export, contract and source-rule checks
as `apack pack validate`. Modules are inspected without activation; generated output is not written.
Dependency details retain the declared spec, exact version, origin, delivery path and content revision. Data availability and executable availability are distinct. Missing generated files produce a reminder to run `apack pack generate-entries`. `--json` emits one validation report with the same dependency inspection frame used for static checks.

Exits 0 when validation is complete and valid, 1 for errors, and 2 when dependency resolution prevents
complete checking. Unchecked work is listed explicitly; incomplete checks are never reported as valid.

#### `apack pack facade-report`

Reports your pack's **facade types** — what packs depending on yours compile against, the same bundle
`apack pack build` writes to `dist/types/pack-types.d.ts` — as a reviewed file at `etc/pack-types.api.md`.

**It needs no build.** It regenerates `src/__generated__/` and bundles the facade itself, so the report is
held against the facade your sources describe now; a `dist` left by an older build is never its subject.
Without `--update` it fails, printing a diff, when the committed report differs; with `--update` it rewrites
the report. Commit the result: the point is that a change to what dependents can see is visible in review
rather than buried in a generated bundle.

After a build, use `--from-build` to compare its verified facade without regeneration or compilation.
It checks sealed output integrity and replays the build's recorded source/dependency inputs; missing,
stale or modified builds fail. This is the root repository's `npm run facade:check` path. The pack-local
script still derives from sources by default. `--skip-generate` instead derives from previously generated
entries and checks their generation stamp. The read-only `--from-build` option cannot be combined
with `--update` or `--skip-generate`.

`apack pack build` warns when your committed report has fallen behind the bundle it just produced. The command
above is what fails, which is why a pack's own CI runs it.

The report is normalised so it moves only when the facade does — imports first and sorted, declarations in
name order, literal unions sorted, and the pack's own path shortened to `.`. That last normalisation matters
for a reason worth knowing: TypeScript prints an inferred union's members in the order it created the member
types, and that order varies between builds, so an unnormalised report would differ from itself.

#### `apack pack info [--json]`

Inspect declared features, entities, steps and services, verified build metadata, compiled content item IDs/descriptions/counts, and dependency provenance. `--json` emits one structured report with the same data as text. Inspection never activates pack modules, downloads dependencies or populates caches.

Build status distinguishes unbuilt, verified, invalid and stale declarations. Compiled content comes from a receipt-checked index; missing or invalid output is unavailable, rather than inferred from source file counts. A verified build proves its output bytes, not that every authored input is unchanged. Dependency details distinguish missing/invalid data from resolved type data whose execution is unavailable.

### Testing

#### `apack pack init-tests`

Scaffold Playwright E2E tests in the pack root: `playwright.config.ts` (tests in `tests/e2e`), `tests/e2e/smoke.spec.ts` (using the first feature with a surface), a `.gitignore` entry for `.apack/`, and `@apackdev/testing` and `@playwright/test` devDependencies. Existing files are kept.

#### `apack pack test [--host <path>] [--prebuilt] [playwright args...]`

Run the pack's Playwright tests in apack. Other arguments go to `playwright test`. The app is, in order:

1. `--host <path|beta>`: an explicit built checkout, `.app` bundle, or downloaded beta
2. `APACK_HOST`: the same selection as an environment default
3. A cached/downloaded beta satisfying the pack's `hostVersion`

Tests always use disposable state and reject profile and secret-copy flags. Contract tests launch no app and reject host flags.

A Beta build is **downloaded once and then reused**: whenever one you already have satisfies the pack's
`hostVersion`, that one runs — so this works offline and asks GitHub nothing. The newest is fetched only when
none of them fits. `apack cache clean` lists what has been downloaded, with sizes, and removes all but the
newest; `--all` removes that one too, which is how you move to a newer Beta.

**`apack pack test` never reads a stored app preference and never asks**, so a test run means the same thing on a fresh machine as on one you have been developing on. Neither command stores a host preference. The fixture builds the pack with the same CLI and installs it into a fresh data dir for each worker, so a run leaves nothing behind either.

`--prebuilt` installs the build already in `dist/` instead of making a new one, for a pipeline that built the
pack in an earlier step. It verifies the sealed output and rechecks the recorded source, linked inputs,
the dependency files the build read, dependency package membership and resolution observations. Timestamp-only touches pass; changed or missing inputs
and damaged output fail with a rebuild instruction. `--prebuilt --release` requires output made with
`apack pack build --release`. The recorded compiler/execution context identifies the selected build;
the Playwright runner's environment is not compared to the compiler's environment. Use this when an
earlier pipeline step owns the build; the test fixture verifies it without rebuilding.

### Distribution

#### `apack pack release [patch|minor|major] [--beta] [--dry-run] [--local] [--skip-tests] [--skip-e2e]`

Cut a release (default `patch`):

1. Preflight: valid manifest with `hostVersion`, dependencies resolve, a clean git tree on the default branch, not behind `origin`, and the tag not already on `origin`
2. Bump `apack.json` and `package.json`. `--beta` follows the app's cycle: `1.2.3` → `1.2.4-beta.0` → `1.2.4-beta.1` → `1.2.4`
3. `apack pack build --release`, `tsc --noEmit`, the `test` script (skip with `--skip-tests`), and `apack pack test` when `playwright.config.ts` exists (skip with `--skip-e2e`)
4. Commit, pack into `.apack/release/`, tag `v<version>` and push

The scaffolded `.github/workflows/release.yml` publishes the GitHub release from the tag. `--local` publishes from this machine instead; it needs `GITHUB_TOKEN` or `GH_TOKEN` and refuses when the workflow exists. `--dry-run` edits no files, runs no git operations and publishes nothing: it builds and verifies the next version's pack under `.apack/release/`.

#### `apack pack release publish [--dir <dir>] [--dry-run]`

Verify the pack in `<dir>` (default `.apack/release`) and create the GitHub release `v<version>` (a prerelease for prerelease versions), uploading `<id>-<version>.tgz`, `.sha256` and `.integrity.json`. The release workflow runs it. Needs `GITHUB_TOKEN` (or `GH_TOKEN`), and `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` or a GitHub `origin` remote.

#### `apack pack install <source> --host <path|beta> [--profile <name>]`

Install a pack into the app's data dir (`<userDataDir>/packs/<id>`). `<source>` is one of:

| Source | Example |
|---|---|
| Local directory (a built pack source or a pack layout) | `../my-pack` |
| Local archive (`.tgz`, `.tar.gz`, `.zip`) | `./my-pack-0.1.0.tgz` |
| URL to a `.tgz`, `.tar.gz` or `.zip` | `https://example.com/my-pack-0.1.0.tgz` |
| GitHub release: `owner/repo`, or `owner/repo@tag` (default: latest) | `user/my-pack@v0.1.0` |

```bash
apack pack install ./my-pack-0.1.0.tgz --host /Applications/apack.app
apack pack install ../my-pack --host /path/to/apack-checkout
apack pack install user/my-pack --host /Applications/apack.app
```

Ordinary install requires `--host` or an associated `APACK_HOST`, `APACK_HOST_ROOT` or
`APACK_HOST_EXECUTABLE`. The source app's advertised default IDs are reserved even before first launch,
when disabled/failed, or after removal. Use `pack replace <id> <source>` to choose your own pack in one
of those slots. Cwd and `--profile` never choose the source app. Selection is offline and does not
activate packs, download a beta, or launch an app. Explicit selection wins over an associated handoff.

A GitHub release needs a `.tgz` asset and the `.sha256` asset published beside it (`apack pack release` writes both); a release without one is refused, since nothing would say the download is that release. A URL install is unverified, and says so. The pack is verified before it's placed, and `hostVersion` is checked against the version the app recorded in that data dir. A source directory must be built: one with neither a `integrity.json` nor a `dist/runtime/index.cjs` beside `dist/types/snapshot.json` is refused, with a note to run `apack pack build` first. Restart the app after installing.

#### `apack pack replace <id> <source> [--profile <name>]`

Deliberately replace the named pack using any source supported by `pack install`. The incoming
manifest must claim that exact ID. The installed build becomes user-managed, so app refreshes
preserve it. An advertised app-default ID or app-managed incumbent refuses ordinary `pack install` and points to this command.
Replacement can also fill an explicitly named missing slot; it preserves stored database overrides.

```bash
apack pack replace default-setup ./my-default-setup
```

#### `apack pack restore <id> --host <path|beta> [--profile <name>]`

Restore a pack from the selected app's shipped builds, re-enable it and resume app-managed updates.
This clears deliberate-removal suppression and preserves stored settings/content overrides.

```bash
apack pack restore default-setup --host /Applications/apack.app
apack pack restore default-setup --host /path/to/apack-checkout --profile my-work
```

`--host` selects the source app; `--profile` independently selects stored state. An associated
`APACK_HOST_ROOT`, `APACK_HOST_EXECUTABLE` or `APACK_HOST` can supply the source when no flag is given.
The current directory does not select a host. An explicit flag wins over an associated handoff.
A checkout needs the pack's build output, not a running app. `--host beta` uses a compatible cached
beta and refuses if none is cached. Restore never downloads or launches an app.

The running app offers the same choices in **Packs**: disable or remove an installed pack, replace it
from its detail view or use **Replace by ID**, and restore an available app default. Replacing chooses
user-managed updates; restoring re-enables the default and resumes app updates. Both keep stored
settings. Host settings remain available when the shipped default is disabled or removed.
App-managed installations show **Update from app** when the verified app source changes, including
a changed build with the same version. Updating preserves disabled state; restoring enables the pack.
User-managed forks receive no app-source update offer.

#### `apack pack uninstall <id> [--profile <name>]`

Remove an installed pack by ID, retaining database settings and recording deliberate removal so boot does not put an app-shipped default back. Use `pack restore` to reinstate the default.

#### `apack pack list [--profile <name>]`

Show installed packs.

`pack install`, `pack replace`, `pack restore`, `pack uninstall` and `pack list` select stored data with `--profile production|development|beta|preview|test`. The default follows the bundled CLI's channel, or production for a standalone CLI. They do not launch an executable. Install and restore separately select source host builds with `--host` or an associated host. Explicit named replacement needs no source-host selection.

Close the app using the selected profile before installing, replacing, restoring, uninstalling, or upgrading packs. These mutations share the app's storage lock with database operations, so concurrent changes are refused. Use `apack pack dev` for live development updates.

### App

#### `apack open [--channel production|beta|preview]`

Open the installed app or bring it to the front. Production is always the default, including
from a beta-bundled CLI. macOS only. No debugging connection is enabled.

#### `apack doctor [--channel production|beta|preview]`

Inspect the installed app's identity, version, executable, data permissions and API listener.
Production is the default. A closed app is normal. Nothing is launched or modified, and no
debugging connection is opened. Failures exit 1. Pack checks are `apack pack doctor`.

#### `apack upgrade [version] [--channel production|beta] [--relaunch] [--force]`

Upgrade the installed app to the indicated version or latest published release. Production
is the default; `--channel beta` selects published prereleases. macOS on Apple Silicon only.

It takes the release's `.zip` and checks it against the `.sha256` published beside it, then expands it with
`ditto` — which keeps the bundle's symlinks, permissions and code signature. Nothing is installed until that
check passes, and the app already in `/Applications` is moved aside rather than deleted, so a failed install
puts it back.

It asks the running app to quit and waits for it to say it has, by the `app.lock` the app removes on
shutdown; a copy that will not quit stops the upgrade rather than being killed, because replacing a bundle
under a live process is the thing being avoided. Nothing here needs a GitHub token — the releases are public
— though `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GH_TOKEN` is used for the higher API rate limit if one is set.

Already-current is reported rather than reinstalled; `--force` installs anyway, and `--relaunch` opens the
app afterwards.

### Database

`apack db` reads and changes the app's database (EARS on LMDB) from the command line: to look at data, repair it when the app can't start, or move it between machines.

```bash
apack db query "return query(EARS.Entity.Note).count()"
apack db inspect Flow-123 --depth 2
apack db runs                               # the latest flow runs
apack db export --out ./export
apack db import ./apack-backup-2026-09-17 --profile production --force
apack db reset --profile production        # lists what it would delete
```

**Which data.** `--profile production|development|beta|preview|test` selects an app data namespace, `--data-dir <path>` any data dir, such as a copy of the user's, or `--profile <name>` a profile `apack pack dev` made, by the name it printed. Name one of them, not two. `--schema-from <path>` names a pack snapshot for a data dir that publishes none of its own. Without it such a dir still opens to **read**, and the command says which entity types it could not name; a command that **changes** it is refused, because an incomplete schema makes a write land on the wrong rows. A command that only reads takes the production app's data without being told, and a dry run of `import`, `reset` or `clear-settings` counts as reading; **a change (`exec`, `repl --write`, and those three with `--force`) names its data dir**, so the user's own data is never what a forgotten flag hits. Each command prints the data dir it opens (on stderr, so results on stdout stay clean). A flag means that app's own data dir, whatever `APACK_USER_DATA_DIR` is set to in the shell; the variable applies only when nothing names a data dir.

Installed schema sources must be complete verified pack builds, with matching manifest, snapshot,
receipt and directory owner. `--schema-from` accepts a complete snapshot in the current format with a
matching declaration revision; a bare manifest or partial fragment is refused. These reads never load
pack runtimes.

**While the app runs.** The commands open the database files themselves (offline); the app is the database's only writer while it runs. So a change (`exec`, `repl --write`, and `import`, `reset` or `clear-settings` with `--force`) refuses while an apack app runs on the data dir: the API it published is running, or (on macOS and Linux) its single-instance lock is held by a live process. Files left behind by a crash name processes that have exited, so they don't stand in the way. Quit the app first. Reading commands work, with a warning that they miss what the app hasn't written yet, and so do the dry runs: they open the database without writing to it, so they also work against a copy you have no permission to change.

While a command changes the database it holds a lock on the data dir (`db-write.lock`), so a second `apack db` is refused and an apack started meanwhile refuses to open that database instead of overwriting the change. A lock left behind by a command that was killed is ignored once its process is gone.

**The run history.** What each flow run did is not in the database: it is the run history, a store of its own beside it (`run-history`), which `apack db runs` reads. Backups, `import` and `reset` cover it with the database, and the app keeps 30 days of it.

**Writing.** There is no apply command: apack content each pack's data when it starts (and `apack pack dev` re-applies a pack it rebuilds), so start the app rather than content a data dir by hand.

**Installed packs.** Entity types, relation kinds and where each type is stored come from the packs installed in the data dir — every enabled pack in `packs/`, the ones the app ships included, read from its own `apack.json`; no pack code runs. A data dir with no packs installed knows only the names the app itself declares, which is the truth about it rather than a degraded reading of it.

#### `apack db query <code> | --file <path> [-o pretty|json|csv] [--out <file>]`

Run query code with the Database console's read helpers: `query` (with `query.withTrashed` and `query.trashed`), `EARS`, `getRow`, `getAttr`, `getRoles`, `findRelations`, `getSchemaStats`. The code is a function body, as in the console: `return` the result. `EARS.Entity` holds the installed packs' entity types. It runs as a plain function, so it can't use top-level `await`, `import` or `require` — a script (`apack db script`) can.

```bash
apack db query "return query(EARS.Entity.Settings).pickAll()" -o json --out settings.json
apack db query --file ./report.js -o csv
```

#### `apack db exec <code> | --file <path> [-o pretty|json|csv] [--out <file>]` (names its data dir)

Run transaction code with the console's read and write helpers (`create`, `upsert`, `write` and `removeRelation`; `write(id)` sets, links, grants, trashes and destroys an entity, and `removeRelation(relationId)` removes one relation). The code runs as one transaction: if it throws part way, none of its writes are kept, and the failure says so. It is synchronous — `await` doesn't parse, and code returning a promise is refused — since an await would split the transaction. A write that fails to reach the files fails the command.

```bash
apack db exec "write('Note-123').set('title', 'Renamed')"
```

#### `apack db repl [--write]` (`--write` names its data dir)

Run console code a line at a time and print each result: query code, or with `--write` transaction code, whose changes are written on exit. `.exit` or Ctrl+D quits.

#### `apack db script <file> [--read-only] [-o pretty|json|csv] [--out <file>] [-- <script arguments>]` (names its data dir)

Run a script file against the database, for work a one-liner can't do: it imports what it likes and brings its own helpers. JavaScript (`.mjs`, `.js`, `.cjs`) runs as it is; TypeScript is compiled first, to a temp file rather than your own directory, with its relative imports compiled in and its packages resolved from where the script lives, so `import.meta` and every import still point where you'd expect. The file default-exports a function, which is called with the open database and whose result is printed like a query's.

```ts
// notes-report.ts
export default async ({ db, EARS, args, log }) => {
  const notes = db.ears.query(EARS.Entity.Note).ids();
  log(`${notes.length} notes`);
  return notes.map((id) => db.ears.getRow(id));
};
```

```bash
apack db script ./notes-report.ts --profile production -o json --out notes.json
apack db script ./cleanup.ts --profile development -- --older-than 30
```

| It receives | |
|---|---|
| `db` | the open database: `query` (`query`, `create`, `upsert`, `write`), `admin`, `store`, `schema`, `paths`, `userDataDir` |
| `EARS` | the entity types and relation kinds of the packs installed in that data dir |
| `args` | whatever follows `--` |
| `log` | prints a line, like the script's own output |

The database is handed to the script rather than left for it to open: the published CLI carries its own copy of the engine, so a script importing `@apackdev/ears` itself would get a second one, with no data in it. `--read-only` opens the database without writing, so a reporting script can run while apack is open.

#### `apack db inspect [<entity-id> | --type <Entity>] [--depth <n>] [--incoming] [--outgoing]`

Print an entity, its roles and its relations grouped by kind, following them `--depth` levels (default 1); `--incoming` or `--outgoing` shows one direction. `--type` prints the first five entities of a type. With neither, it prints entities and relations per entity type.

#### `apack db runs [--run <id>] [--flow <id>] [--limit <n>] [--json]`

List the flow runs in the run history, newest first (20 unless `--limit` says otherwise): each session's root and every flow it ran, one line each with its id, status, start time, label and the flow it ran. `--flow` lists one flow's runs, and `--json` prints the list as JSON. `--run <id>` prints that run node and everything under it — the events it heard, the steps they ran, each with what it was given and what it returned — as one JSON tree. It opens the run history read-only, so it works while apack runs (with the usual warning) and changes nothing.

#### `apack db export --out <dir> [--type <Entity>...] [--format json|csv]`

Write each entity type's entities, with every attribute, to `<dir>/<Entity>.json` (or `.csv`), and a summary (when it ran, the data dir, the format and the counts) to `<dir>/export.json`. Without `--type`, every type with entities and the relations, to `<dir>/Relation.json` (each `{ id, kind, source, target, info }`; `Relation` is the engine's own name, which no entity type can take), with their count as the summary's `relations`. Roles are in each entity's `role` attribute.

#### `apack db import <backup-dir> [--force] [--skip-unknown]` (names its data dir)

Replace the database and the run history the backup holds, and the media folder when it has one, with a backup made in the Database settings' Backup & Restore. The backup is checked first: it has `metadata.json`, lists the app's main database, that folder is there, and every database it would put in place opens in a storage format this version reads — so a backup this apack can't read is refused before any of your data is replaced. A backup made by a newer apack may also hold stores this one doesn't have; importing it would replace your data with an incomplete copy, so it's refused unless you pass `--skip-unknown`, which imports it without them. If the backup lists a store it holds nothing for, the listing says so and that store comes back empty. Without `--force` it lists the backup, its contents and what it would replace, and changes nothing. The app migrates the data on its next start if the backup is from an earlier version.

#### `apack db reset [--force] [--keep-keys]` (names its data dir)

Delete all of the app's data, as Reset Database in the Database settings does: the database, the run history and the stored secrets. The app creates its default data (settings, written flows, the packs' content) on its next start and shows onboarding. Without `--force` it lists the entities per type and each stored secret it would delete.

Close tools reading or writing the run history before a forced reset; it refuses them before deleting data.
A reset interrupted between its separate stores can leave part of the reset complete. Run it again to finish.

No backup holds the secrets — `export` and the Database settings' backups copy the databases and the media folder, never the secrets or the data key that encrypts them — so a deleted secret is entered again in Settings → Secrets. That's why the listing names each one by provider and label (never its value), and why `--keep-keys` leaves them where they are and deletes only the data.

#### `apack db clear-settings [--force]` (names its data dir)

Destroy every Settings row (the user's changes to the default settings); the app recreates the defaults on its next start. Without `--force` it lists each row and the settings it stores.

In the apack repo, `npm run db:query`, `db:exec`, `db:repl`, `db:inspect`, `db:runs`, `db:export`, `db:import`, `db:reset` and `db:clear-settings` run these commands on the development app's data (`-d`): `npm run db:query -- "return query.all().count()"`.

### Cleanup

#### `apack profiles`

Every apack data dir on this machine, and the verbs for the ones you made. Works outside a pack — a
data dir belongs to you rather than to any pack.

```
apack profiles                  what exists
apack profiles --sizes          with a size column
apack profiles --all            include the throwaway dirs `run --fresh --rm` makes
apack profiles new [name]       create one; a name is minted if you don't give one
apack profiles rename <a> <b>   rename one
apack profiles rm <name>...     remove the ones you name
apack profiles rm --leaked      remove the ones a killed run left behind
apack profiles trim [<name>...] reclaim the caches Chromium rebuilds, in any data dir
apack profiles stop <name>      close the app running on one (or --all)
```

Two kinds of directory, listed apart. An **environment** is where an app of that channel keeps its data —
production, beta, development, test — and nothing here removes one; a row says whether an app has it open,
what version last wrote to it, and `(no app data)` when the directory holds only a Chromium profile. A
**profile** is a data dir you can throw away.

**`trim` is how you get the disk back, including from an environment nothing removes.** It deletes seven
directories — `Cache`, `Code Cache`, `GPUCache`, `DawnGraphiteCache`, `DawnWebGPUCache`, `Shared Dictionary`,
`blob_storage` — and nothing else. Your notes, settings, installed packs and the in-app browser's logins are
untouched, so it asks for no confirmation. A dir with an app running on it is skipped, those files being
open. With no names it does every dir there is.

**How much it frees depends on which dir**, which is worth knowing before you run it: a development dir is
mostly cache and a production one mostly is not. Measured 2026-10-10, 1.3GB came back from a 1.6GB
development dir and 13MB from a 1.4GB production one — the difference being the in-app browser's logged-in
sessions and your own media and database, which no command here deletes. For those, `apack db export`
first, then `apack db reset --force` if you mean it.

**`stop` closes the app on a data dir**, by name or `--all`, and waits for the dir to come free. The pid
comes from what the app published about itself rather than from a search for a matching process.

Sizes are behind a flag because taking them means walking every directory: measured, 674ms for a 1.4GB
production dir and 1255ms for a 1.5GB development one. Names and paths come back immediately.

A profile an app is currently running on is never renamed or removed: taking a data dir away from a
running app does not stop it, it makes the app write the directory back.

#### `apack pack clean`

Remove build output: `dist/`, `.apack/`, `src/__generated__/`.

#### `apack cache clean [--all]`

Lists the apack Beta builds `--host beta` downloaded — a few hundred megabytes each, one per
release tested against — and removes all but the newest, which is the one a later run would reuse; `--all`
removes every build. It works outside a pack.

Data dirs are `apack profiles`, below: what exists, and removing the ones you own.

### Desktop app installation

```bash
apack install                       # Latest stable production release
apack install 0.4.0                 # Specific production release (v0.4.0 also works)
apack install --replace             # Explicitly replace an existing app
apack upgrade                       # Update an installed app to the latest stable release
apack upgrade 0.4.0 --force          # Explicit reinstall or downgrade
apack uninstall                     # Remove the app bundle; keep data and settings
apack install --channel beta                    # Latest beta, installed separately
```

These commands manage `/Applications/apack.app` (or `apack Beta.app` with `--channel beta`) on macOS Apple Silicon. App commands default to production even when invoked from the beta app. Pack installation is `apack pack install <source>`; pack removal is `apack pack uninstall <id>`.

Downloads must have a matching published SHA-256 checksum. An incomplete latest release fails rather than silently installing an older version. The downloaded bundle's identity, executable and version are checked before the existing app is asked to quit. Replacement is staged on the destination filesystem and restores the previous bundle if the swap fails. A concurrent app operation is refused. `install` refuses any existing bundle without `--replace`; `upgrade` requires an existing app and skips a same-version or older release unless `--force` is supplied. `--relaunch` opens the installed app after install or upgrade. Uninstall never deletes databases, packs, profiles or settings.

### Inspecting pack declarations

`apack pack info` lists declared features and their systems, services, repositories and reference
identities, plus extension kinds, lifecycle hooks, migrations, entities, relations and content keys.
It reads verified compiled inventory separately and reports unbuilt, stale or invalid output without
activating pack modules. Feature-owned services appear under their feature; pack services appear under
extensions.

`apack pack info --json` returns the complete validated manifest in `declared`, retaining its keyed
maps, ownership, module targets and metadata. It does not replace declarations with a selected list of
names. `build` describes verified output and compiled content; `dependencies` describes inspection of
declared dependencies. Authored declarations and verified output may differ in a stale build, which
is reported explicitly. Neither inspection mode executes pack code or creates user data.

# Content

A pack's content is source files compiled to JSON at build time and written into the database when the pack is installed or updated. `apack.json` `content.sources` names each one.

A declared specialty source (`actions`, `prompts`, `flows`, `documents` or `commands`) must exist; a missing path fails the build.
Completed builds validate the content index against the manifest: compiled sources are written entries,
datasets are non-written entries, and each has its compiled JSON file. Applier-only sources read their
own data and have no compiled index entry. Build publication, staging and installation refuse missing
or contradictory inventories without executing pack modules.

documents.body:
## The four stages

A pack's content passes through four, and each has its own vocabulary. **The content is the noun. The two verbs are `apply`, which the app does, and `import`, which the user asks for.**

| Stage | What happens | Named |
|---|---|---|
| **author** | you write the sources | `src/content/`, `content.sources`, `content.formats`, `content.writers` |
| **compile** | `apack pack build` turns them into items and hashes each one | `dist/runtime/content/*.content.json`, `content.json`, `contentHash` |
| **apply** | the app writes those items into the database, and converges them on every upgrade | `applyPacks()`, a `ContentApplier`'s `apply()`, `ApplyResult` |
| **import** | the user asks for the content back, which reads none of the record below | `importContent()`, `ImportMode`, `ImportResult` |
| **record** | the app remembers what it last wrote, part by part, so your edits survive the next import | `contentKey`, the pack's applied content |

Three things follow from the split that are easy to conflate. Editing a content source changes its `contentHash` at
**compile**, and that is what makes the next **apply** rewrite the entity — so a change with no visible effect on
the content still reaches every user who has not edited that entity. **Apply and import are different operations**:
an apply never overwrites the user's work, and an import is the user asking for the content back and does. And this
repo's `content-parity` goldens record what an apply *produces*: re-recording them
(`npm run content-parity:update -w @app/default-setup`) rewrites a test expectation and no user data.

The SDK compiles three content keys itself:

- **Actions** — async functions that do work (call LLMs, query data, emit events)
- **Prompts** — parameterized text templates for LLM calls
- **Flows** — declarative event-driven workflows that orchestrate actions

A feature's default settings go in `features.<id>.settings` (see [Feature settings](manifest.md#feature-settings)); the settings entity and its content are default-setup's (its `settings` entry and format).

Any other entity type — yours, a dependency's, or the SDK's — is written from markdown or JSON with a format and a content source in `apack.json`, and no SDK code (see [Writing entities](#writing-entities)).

documents.body:
### How an action runs

The compiled body of `action` runs in one sandbox, whether a flow's action step runs it or another action calls it through `services.action` (`executeAction`, `executeIfFound`). It receives:

- `params`: the step's resolved input (or the params the caller passed)
- `services`: the object below, with `services.logger` named `action:<label>`, so the Logs view shows which action logged
- `z`: zod, for schemas
- `flowId`: the running flow's run node id when a flow step runs it; `undefined` otherwise
documents.name: content / Content / Actions / How an action runs

documents.body:
### Available services

Actions receive the accepted service view supplied by their executing pack, with an attributed logger and emitter. The default-setup action runner supplies its own declared services and selected host APIs. The tables below describe that runner.

Ordinary pack source imports its own `services` and `Services` from `#generated/services.ts`: own services and the SDK baseline are implicit, while host/dependency APIs require `consumes.services`. Depending on default-setup alone does not grant its services. See [service selection](services-and-data.md#services).

**default-setup's services**

| Service | Description |
|---|---|
| `services.chat` | Chat messages and blocks (`sendBlockMessage`, `sendSystemMessage`, `sendChoiceBlock`, `sendQuestionBlock`, `createThreadAndNotify`, …) |
| `services.threads` | Thread chat state (`updateChatState`) |
| `services.artifact` | Artifact creation and updates (`createAndNotify`, `updateAndNotify`, `findOrCreateByType`) |
| `services.library` | Library documents and folders (`find`, `findByCode`, `findByName`, `findByPath`, `getText`, `list`, `create`, `update`, `createFolder`, `rename`, `move`, `remove`). The chat's slash commands are not here: they are a derivation over stored documents, read with `getCommands()` (see [Slash commands](#slash-commands)) |
| `services.prompt` | Prompt templates (`usePrompt`, `findByLabel`) |
| `services.action` | Look up and run actions (`findByLabel`, `executeAction`, `executeIfFound`) |
| `services.brain` | Ad-hoc brain event listeners (`listen`, `unlisten`) |
| `services.scheduler` | Cron schedules for flow triggers (`registerSchedule`, `unregisterByPrefix`, `clearAllSchedules`) |
| `services.database` | Live-data schema and topology context for AI query generation (`buildQueryContext`) |
| `services.cli` | CLI tools: `git`, `gh`, `claudeCode`, `codex`, plus `testCli` |
| `services.codex` | The Codex app-server (threads, turns, approvals, sessions) |

**Host services**

| Service | Description |
|---|---|
| `services.inference` | Model calls (`generateText`, `streamText`, `createAgent`, `embed`/`embedMany`, `generateImage`, `generateSpeech`, `transcribe`, `rerank`) with the user's provider keys; see [Inference](services-and-data.md#inference) |
| `services.repository` | The pack's declared repositories (queries and commands); actions read and write data through them |
| `services.settings` | Caller-bound preferences: `get(target)`, `set(target, path, value, condition?)`, `reset(target)` and `onChange(listener)`. Targets identify host app, pack-group or feature preferences; target mutation policy still applies |
| `services.logger` | Structured logging, named `action:<label>` |
| `services.emitter` | Typed sends to surfaces and systems (`broadcastToSurface`, and `sendToSystem` naming a system `<pack>/<feature>`, such as `'my-pack/bookmarks'`, or a role, `{ role: 'brain' }`) |
| `services.appData` | Reset, export and import app data, and inspect backup metadata |
| `services.onboarding` | Read and complete onboarding (`isComplete`, `complete`) without granting whole-data administration |
| `services.runHistory` | Flow runs: each run's tree of nodes, recorded while it runs and kept after |
| `services.secrets` | The user's API keys as metadata (`list`, `select`, `rename`, `delete`, `status`); never values |
| `services.filesystem` | Files and folders on disk, as UTF-8 text (`readFile`, `writeFile`, `readDir`, `mkdir`, `stat`, `exists`, `rename`, `remove`) |

### Metadata

`ActionMeta` (`@apackdev/sdk/build`):

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `label` | `string` | The action's name: flow `action` steps and `services.action.findByLabel` find it by label. Two actions with one label fail the build |
| `description` | `string?` | Shown in the Actions UI |
| `category` | `string?` | Groups the action in the Actions UI (`apack pack add action --category`, default the pack id) |
| `input` | `Record<string, ActionParameter>` | The parameters, by name |
| `output` | `unknown?` | A description of the result, stored with the action |

`ActionParameter`: `type` (`'string' \| 'number' \| 'boolean' \| 'object' \| 'array' \| 'any'`), `description?`, `required?`, `default?`, `placeholder?`. These describe the parameters; nothing validates `params` against them or fills in `default` when the action runs.

documents.body:
### Parameters

The build keeps only the function's body, and the runtime calls it with fixed parameter names, so keep them named `params`, `services`, `z` and `flowId`:

| Parameter | From a flow `action` step | From `services.action.executeAction(actionFn, params)` / `executeIfFound(label, params)` |
|---|---|---|
| `params` | The step's `params`, overridden by its resolved `map` (see [Mappings](#mappings)) | `params` |
| `services` | The app's `services` | The app's `services` |
| `z` | zod | `undefined` |
| `flowId` | The running flow's run node id | `undefined` |

The function's return value is the step's result (`$.lastStep.result`).

documents.body:
### Rules

The build bundles each action file with esbuild and extracts its `meta` and the body of `action`:

- **Imports**: a relative import is bundled into the action. The only package import allowed is `@apackdev/sdk/actions` (`formatProviderError(error, provider, alternatives?)`, `buildTranscript(messages, { maxMessages?, maxChars? })`); any other package, `node:` modules included, fails the build. Type-only imports (`ActionMeta`, `Services`, `Z`) are erased and always allowed.
- **Node globals** (`require`, `process`, `__dirname`, `__filename`, `Buffer`, `global`) in the bundled code only produce a build warning, but the action runs in the app's backend without them.
- **`meta` is evaluated on its own**: write it as an object literal that references no imports or other variables.
- **Top-level helpers** (functions and constants next to `action`) are inlined into the action. A helper function whose only uses are direct calls can declare a `services` parameter: the build removes it and the helper uses the action's `services`.
- **Model calls need no imports**: `output` is data (`{ type: 'object', schema }`, `{ type: 'choice', options }`, …), tools are plain `{ description, inputSchema, execute }` objects, and `stopWhen` is a function. Agents, embeddings, images and speech work the same way (`services.inference.createAgent`, `embed`, `generateImage`, …). See [Inference](services-and-data.md#inference).
- **Scanning**: every `.ts` file under the directory, subdirectories included, is compiled when it has a line starting `export const meta`. Other files (shared helpers) and `*.example.ts` files are skipped. A `_` prefix doesn't skip an action file.

### Rules

- `template(params, usePrompt)` must be **synchronous** and return a string. Keep the parameters named `params` and `usePrompt`: the build keeps only the body.
- `usePrompt(label, params)` renders another prompt by label (up to 10 levels deep), returning `undefined` when there's none.

documents.body:
### Flow definitions

A flow file's default export is a `FlowDSL` (`@apackdev/sdk/build`): flow name → a `Track[]`, or a `FlowConfig`.

| Type | Fields |
|---|---|
| `FlowConfig` | `tracks: Track[]`; `root?: boolean` marks the root flow, which the brain starts when the app starts (at most one; default-setup's `Root Flow` is the app's); `contentHash?` is written by the build, a hash of `tracks` and `root` |
| `Track` | One trigger field (`event` for a listener, `schedule` for a schedule), `label?`, `description?`, `exits: DSLStepNode[][]` (each exit a chain of steps, run in parallel) |
| `DSLNodeBase` | Options every step helper takes: `label?`, `description?`, `final?`, `next?` |

Every other flow runs as a subflow that a running flow spawned: default-setup's `Root Flow` spawns its long-running work modes from its entry track. An event reaches every running flow (see `fire`'s `scope`).

The root also receives `client.ready` once per run after this pack's frontend has become available.
If the frontend was already seen when a root starts or restarts, that new root receives readiness too.
This is a lifecycle signal to that root actor, not a broadcast or a count of live connections. Reconnects
and additional windows do not repeat it in the same run. A paused root defers the signal; replacing or
stopping the root discards its pending delivery. A data restore leaves the root stopped until explicitly
started. Default-setup's authored root uses readiness to check host onboarding completion and start or
resume its onboarding workflow; a custom root need not do so. Backend flow entry can run before any
frontend exists, when frontend sends are ignored, so presentation-dependent startup belongs behind
readiness rather than an unconditional entry track.

**A worked example of the exported form** lives in the apack repo at
`packages/default-setup/tests/extensions/steps/__golden__/exported-flows.json` — what
`exportFlowsToDSL` writes for a flow that uses every step default-setup registers, including a
`FlowConfig` with `root`, the `exits` nesting and a `subflow` reference. It is recorded by the spec
beside it rather than kept by hand, so it cannot drift from the types: re-record it with
`npm run flow-export:update -w @app/default-setup`, and never edit it.

A step's options:

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `label` | The node's label. Defaults per step (the action or prompt name, the event, the flow name, `Create <entity>`, `Switch <index>`, …). Labels are unique within a flow, across its tracks, branches and track labels: a duplicate fails the build (`Duplicate step label`), so label repeated steps, and give a step an explicit label when its default matches an `on()` track's (`fire('x')` beside `on('x', …)`) |
| `description` | Stored on the node, shown in the editor |
| `final` | When this step completes, the flow completes with the step's result (a subflow's result becomes its step's result in the parent) |
| `next` | Continues at the node with this label in the same flow instead of the next step in the chain; an unknown label fails validation |

A flow without a `final` step completes when all its tracks drain, unless it has a `schedule` track. `keepAlive()` never completes, so its track never drains.
documents.name: content / Content / Flows / Flow definitions

documents.body:
### Flow helpers

`#generated/flow-helpers` exports `entry` and `on` from the SDK, a helper per step with a `dsl` entry in the manifest, and a track builder per trigger other than `event` (see [Flow helpers](extensions.md#flow-helpers)). A pack gets its dependencies' flow helpers re-exported too: `generate-entries` writes each dependency's as `src/__generated__/deps/<id>.flow-helpers.{js,d.ts}` from its snapshot. Each helper's `opts` is typed from its step's `DSL…Node` interface.

default-setup's helpers:

| Helper | Step type | Options (besides `label`, `description`, `final`, `next`) | Does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `entry(...exits)` | `listener` track | — | The `flow.entry` track, run when the flow starts. Each argument is a chain; several run in parallel. Needs at least one (`entry([keepAlive()])`) |
| `on(event, exits, label?)` | `listener` track | — | Runs `exits` when the flow receives `event`. `label` defaults to the event |
| `schedule(cron, exits, label?)` | `schedule` track | — | Runs `exits` on a cron schedule (5 or 6 fields, checked at build) while the flow runs. `label` defaults to `Schedule (<cron>)`. The flow doesn't complete when its tracks drain |
| `action(action, opts?)` | `action` | `map?: Record<string, string>`, `params?: Record<string, any>` | Runs the action with this label; the result is its return value. The label must be an action this pack's `actions` content compiles |
| `llm(prompt, opts?)` | `llm` | `map?`, `model?: ModelId` (`provider:model`, default `anthropic:claude-opus-5`), `temperature?`, `maxTokens?`, `systemPrompt?` | Renders the prompt with this label with the mapped params and calls `services.inference.generateText`. Result `{ text, usage, finishReason, warnings? }`. The label must be a prompt this pack's `prompts` content compiles |
| `fire(event, opts?)` | `fire` | `scope?: 'local' \| 'global'` (default `local`), `payload?: unknown` | Sends `event` with `payload`: its `$.` strings are resolved at any depth of objects and arrays (`'$.lastStep.result'` gives the value itself), other values are literal. `local` sends to the flow running the step, `global` to every running flow; `services.brain` listeners get it in either scope, with `targetFlowId` set for `local`. Result `{ eventFired, eventScope, targetFlowId, payload }` |
| `subflow(flow, opts?)` | `subflow` | `inherit?: boolean` (default `true`), `map?` | Starts the flow with this name and completes when it does. Its `flow.entry` event data holds the mapped fields (`$.event.data.<target>`). With `inherit` it also holds the parent track's event data (a mapped field wins), and the entry track starts with the parent track's steps, so `$.lastStep` and `$.steps[label=…]` read the parent's until the subflow runs its own |
| `branch(conditions, else?, label?)` | `switch` | — | `conditions: { if: string; steps: DSLStepNode[] }[]`, `else?: DSLStepNode[]`. Runs the steps of the first condition that matches (see [Switch conditions](#switch-conditions)), else `else`; with no match and no `else` the chain ends. After a branch's steps, the chain continues with the step after the switch |
| `keepAlive(label?)` | `keep_alive` | — | Never completes: keeps its track, and the flow, running |
| `kill(label = 'Kill Flow')` | `kill` | — | Stops the flow running the step |
| `query(prompt, opts?)` | `query` | `as?: string` (default `rows`, not `query`), `model?: ModelId` (default `anthropic:claude-opus-5`) | The model turns `prompt` into a read-only EARS query, instructed by the `DB Query System` prompt with `services.database.buildQueryContext()`, and the step runs it with the database console's read-only executor. Result `{ query, [as]: value }`. Fails when the model can't be called, returns no query, or the query fails or writes |
| `create(entity, opts?)` | `create` | `map?`, `params?: Record<string, unknown>` (literal fields; mapped fields win), `inferLabel?: boolean` (default `true`) | Creates an entity of type `entity`, which must be registered in the running app (`isEntityType`: the SDK's or any registered pack's). Without a `label` field, the label comes from `title`, `name` or `topic`, else `New <Entity> <n>`. Result the created row |
| `update(target, opts?)` | `update` | `map?`, `params?`, `onMissing?: 'fail' \| 'ignore' \| 'create'` (default `fail`), `entity?: string` | Writes the fields to the entity with id `target`: a `$.` path resolved when the step runs (`$.lastStep.result.id` after a `create`; `$.lastStep.id` is the step's run-history node, not an entity, so an update to it finds none) or a literal id. A `null` field drops it. Result the row with `updated: true`. With no such entity, `fail` errors naming the id, `ignore` results `{ updated: false }`, and `create` creates an `entity` (required at build) with the fields, result the row with `updated: false, created: true` |
| `transform(script, opts?)` | `transform` | `outputType?: 'json' \| 'text' \| 'custom'` (default `json`), `map?` | `script` is an async function body run as an action runs (`services.action.executeAction`), with `services` and `params`: `params.input` is the previous step's result, then the mapped fields (a mapped `input` replaces it). Result: `json` the returned value round-tripped through JSON (fails if it isn't serializable), `text` `String(value)`, `custom` the value as returned. A script error fails the step with `Transform step "<label>" script failed: <message>` |

`action`, `llm`, `fire`, `subflow`, `create` and `update` option names come from their `DSL…Node` interfaces in `packages/default-setup/src/extensions/steps/<step>/types.ts`.

documents.body:
### Mappings

A step's `map` is `{ target: source }`. Each source is resolved when the step runs:

- A string starting `$.` is a path into the step's execution context. `[field=value]` picks an array item.
- Any other string is parsed as JSON when it parses (`'3'` → `3`, `'true'` → `true`), otherwise used as a literal string.
- A value that resolves to `undefined` is passed as `undefined`.

An `action` step's `params`, and a `create` or `update` step's fields, are the step's `params` with the mapped values over them; `llm` renders its prompt with the mapped values.

| Path | Value |
|---|---|
| `$.event.type` | The event that started the track (`flow.entry`, `user.command`, `schedule.<node id>`) |
| `$.event.data` | The event's data |
| `$.event.data.payload` | A sent event's payload: what `fire`'s `payload` holds, or what a client or `runFlow` sent (`$.event.data.payload.text`) |
| `$.event.data.<target>` | In a subflow's `flow.entry` track, the subflow step's mapped field, or, when it inherits, the parent event's field |
| `$.lastStep.result` | The result of the step that ran before this one in the track (`$.lastStep.label` its label) |
| `$.steps[label=<label>].result` | The result of an earlier step in this track, by label (`$.steps[id=<run node id>]` by run node) |

`$.steps` holds only the track's own steps, in the order they completed (a subflow that inherits starts its entry track with the parent track's).
documents.name: content / Content / Flows / Mappings

documents.body:
### Switch conditions

A condition's `if` is `<key> <operator> <value>`:

- **Key**: a `$.` path into the execution context, or a bare key read from the previous step's result (`intent` is `$.lastStep.result.intent`). An `if` with no operator is `<key> == true`.
- **Value**: a `$.` path, `true`/`false`, a number, a quoted string (`'question'`), or otherwise the rest of the text as a string.

| Operator | Matches when |
|---|---|
| `==`, `===` | loosely equal (`==`) |
| `!=`, `!==` | loosely not equal |
| `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` | both sides compared as numbers |
| `contains`, `starts_with`, `ends_with` | the key's value as a string contains, starts or ends with the value |
| `matches` | the value, as a regular expression (up to 500 characters), matches the key's value |
| `is_empty` | the key's value is `null`, `undefined`, `''`, `[]` or `{}` (takes no value) |
| `is_null` | the key's value is `null` or `undefined` (takes no value) |
documents.name: content / Content / Flows / Switch conditions

### Rules

- The default export is the `FlowDSL` object (`export default { ... } satisfies FlowDSL`). Flow files run at build time in Node, so they can import anything; import step helpers from `#generated/flow-helpers`.
- Only the `.ts` files directly in the flows directory are read, not subdirectories. Files starting with `_` and `*.example.ts` files are skipped, so shared flow pieces can live in `_helpers.ts`.
- A flow name defined twice, or more than one `root: true`, fails the build.
- At build time, `action` and `llm` steps must name actions and prompts this pack's own `actions` and `prompts` content compile. At apply time a flow is checked again against every action and prompt in the database; a flow that fails is reported and not written.

documents.body:
### Documents and commands

`documents` and `commands` compile a directory of markdown into the SDK's document model, so any pack ships
documents with no format, writer or dependency of its own. A directory is a `Collection` (its `_meta.md`
frontmatter gives `name` and `description`); a file is a `Document` (frontmatter `name`, `tags: [a, b]` and
`type`). A `<!-- section:<type>[:<param>] -->` marker starts a section — `markdown`, `text`, `code:<language>`,
`field` (`**key**: value` lines) or `list` (`- item` lines) — and a body with no marker is one markdown section.
A `media/` directory at the source's root is copied beside the records, and a document's `media/<file>` links
become its media. `parseDocumentSections` and `serializeDocumentSections` (`@apackdev/sdk/content`) read and
write that syntax for code that imports or exports documents. The two keys differ in one default:
under `commands` a document is a [command list](#slash-commands) unless its `type` says otherwise.
documents.name: content / Content / Manifest configuration / Documents and commands

### Include sets

ContentAppliers take an include set per key (`ContentSelection = true | ReadonlySet<string>`, from `@apackdev/sdk/utils`). `true` or no entry content every item; a set content only the top-level items it names, and an empty set skips the key. The boot apply includes every key; Import Pack Content builds them from the items the user picks. Items are named as `content.json` lists them:

| Key | Item name |
|---|---|
| `actions`, `prompts` | The label |
| `flows` | The flow name |
| `documents`, `commands` | The top-level document's or folder's name |
| A content source | The record's first `identity` field other than `parent`, else its `name`, `title` or `label` |

documents.body:
### Markdown

- Each `.md` file is a record, and `entity` is a single type (`tree.branchEntity` gives directories theirs). Frontmatter is YAML 1.2 (CRLF line endings and a byte order mark are fine), so `title: 2024` reads as a number; `"type": "string"` coerces it back.
- `fields` maps record fields to a source: `body` (the markdown after the frontmatter), `filename` (the file or directory name with dashes as spaces), `path` (relative to the entry's `path`) or `frontmatter.<name>`. `default` applies when the source is absent, `null` or an empty string (`title:` or `title: ""`); `"filename"` as a default means the display name. A field with no value and no `default` is left out of the record. Content track the fields a record sets (see [Change tracking](#change-tracking)), so leave defaults a user may change, like flags, to the entity's defaults or a `create` hook.
- With `tree`, each subdirectory is a parent record (its `branch` file gives its frontmatter and body, `branchEntity` its type) and its files are children, linked with `relKind`. Without `tree`, only the top-level files are read.
- `media` is a directory under the entry's `path`, copied with the content and not read as records (no other directory is skipped); `![alt](media/pic.png)` links in any of a record's text fields (nested values included) are rewritten to the row's `media://<id>/pic.png`.

documents.body:
### Change tracking

Written entities store their item's `contentHash`, and the app keeps, per pack, one entry per entity it has written: a hash per **part** of what it wrote. A part is one addressable piece of the item — a field's name for an ordinary entity; a flow's own fields, each of its nodes, and its wiring. A part is edited when it no longer holds what the applier wrote, whatever changed it (the app's editors, the database console, a flow). Fields an item doesn't set aren't parts: a user can favorite a written note and it still takes updates.

Parts rather than one hash per item is what keeps an edit from spreading. A thirty-step flow has thirty-two parts, so editing one step's description marks that step edited and says so, rather than marking the flow edited with nothing to say what — which used to freeze all thirty of its rows against every later version, silently and for good.

When a changed item no longer sets a field the last apply set (the source dropped `completed: true`), updating the entity resets that field: without hooks the applier drops it from the row, and an `update` hook gets it in `clearedFields` to reset (default-setup's Note hooks reset it to a new note's value). A field no apply of the entity ever set, like a user's favorite, isn't touched.

Written entities also store a `contentKey`: the writing pack's id, the entry key and the record's identity in the source (for a tree, its ancestors' too). An apply finds a row by its `contentKey` first, so a row the user renamed is still found, left as renamed (a renamed row is edited), and not written again as a copy. Two packs' records with the same entry key and identity content a row each. A row without a `contentKey` that matches a record's identity (a user's row with the same name) isn't written again beside it. The pack id comes from `content.json`, which `apack pack build` writes; writing compiled content without it fails until the pack is rebuilt.

Flows follow the same rules, with the parts above: its row's fields, each node's values, and its wiring (independent of the relations' order). Editing a node marks that node, adding or removing one marks it and the wiring, and renaming the flow marks its fields. Moving nodes in the editor doesn't mark anything.

Unlike other entities, a flow's id and its nodes' ids come from the flow's name, so flows can't share a name: a pack's flow isn't written when another pack has already written a flow with its name, or a user's flow has the ids it would write. The existing flow is left as it is and the run reports an error (`Flow "X": a flow with this name already exists (written by <pack>)`, or `(created by the user)`). A user's flow with the name (and its own ids) is left alone as user-owned, as for other entities.

A subflow step naming a flow the same pack writes runs that flow, however the user renamed it, and never another flow with its name. When the pack's apply left a user's or another pack's flow with that name in place of its own, the step runs that flow. Other names run the flow with that label.

Re-applying follows the same rules for every entry:

| Import mode | Existing row |
|---|---|
| `replace-on-collision` (and the boot apply) | Updated only when the stored hash differs and the row isn't edited. A row with no stored hash is treated as user-created, and an edited row is left as it is. Children are still visited. |
| `keep-existing` | Left alone, with its children. |
| `wipe-and-replace` | Every row of the entry's entity types (its format's `entity`) is removed first, whoever created it: the user's rows and other packs' rows of those types too, even when the entry has no records of a type. Then all records are created. |

Rows without a stored `contentHash` (rows users created) stay user-owned, in every mode. A row the app wrote but has no parts for — one written by a version from before it recorded them — is **adopted**: written once and recorded, after which its edits are honoured. That overwrites an edit made before the record existed, which is the trade for not freezing every such row for good.

**A written entity the user threw away is not written again, and nor are its children.** An apply finds its own entity by `contentKey` whether or not it is in the trash (`query.withTrashed`), so a trashed entity (`write(id).trash()`) is one the user has taken ownership of: it is left alone, and its children are not visited — they would be created under a deleted parent. This is the same rule as the ones above, and it means a pack needs no policy to say "write this only on a first run".

**An entity deleted outright is not written again either, because the app remembers writing it.** Nothing is left of it, so what answers for it is the pack's record of what it wrote: a key it wrote with no entity behind it now is one the user removed. The rule holds whatever your feature's delete does — a trashed entity is read directly, a destroyed one through the record.

documents.section: Content / Writing entities / Content you stop shipping
documents.body:
### Content you stop shipping

**A record your content no longer holds is removed from the user's database — unless they edited it.** The same rule as everything above: ours to remove while it is still ours, theirs to decide once they have touched it. Nothing has to be declared: the app holds an entry per row it wrote, so the removals are the entries your new content no longer names.

Three things it will not do. A content key whose compiled file it could not read contributes no removals, because a key that said nothing cannot be diffed against. A removal follows the parent chain, so keeping an edited child keeps the rows above it. And a `container` another pack's rows (or the user's) are filed under is never removed, since removing the folder would take their content with it.

An edited item you stopped shipping is kept, and under an `offer` entry it is named: the user is asked whether to keep it or delete it. Under `theirs` it is simply kept, which is what `theirs` means.

**Removal is per entry key.** Each entry diffs only the keys under its own prefix, so content whose *whole entry* you stop declaring has no writer left to remove it — and renaming an entry key orphans what the old one wrote, leaving the new key's rows beside them.

documents.section: Content / Writing entities / What an import does differently
documents.body:
### What an import does differently

**Settings → Import Pack Content reads none of that record.** Asking for a pack's data back is asking for the rows to come back, so an import creates a row the user deleted, writes over a row they edited, and removes nothing. It leaves rows with no hash of the pack's alone — a row the user created themselves is never the pack's to replace — and it records what it wrote, so the next boot does not read its writes as the user's edits.

`wipe-and-replace` is blunter still, and is not about the record at all: it removes every row of the entry's types first, trashed ones and other packs' included, and creates them all again.

documents.body:
## Slash commands

A slash command is a `/name` an editor's command popup offers. **A command is content**, like an action, a
prompt or a flow: a pack ships them in a content source, the apply writes them into the user's data, and the
user edits them afterwards — with the three-way merge and the offers every other content entry gets. There is
no manifest key that lists commands, and nothing to merge: one source, so a name cannot shadow another.

A command lives in a document whose field section is `**name**: placeholder` lines, and what makes it one is
the document's own `documentType`. **A command is only a document with a type**, so any document that says it
is a command list is served as one, and a document that says nothing is just a document.

A file declares it in frontmatter (`type: commands`), and the **content key** supplies a default where a whole
source is one kind — so a file in a `commands` source cannot fail to be a command list by saying nothing, while
a file that declares something else is what it says:

| source's key | the file's `type:` | `documentType` |
|---|---|---|
| `commands` | absent | `commands` |
| `commands` | `type: notes` | `notes` |
| `documents` | absent | none — just a document |
| `documents` | `type: commands` | `commands`, served with the rest |

default-setup's are `src/content/commands/internal/*.md`, under its `commands` key. Any pack declares the same
key (`"commands": "src/content/commands"`) and gets the same rows, with no dependency. A name two documents
define keeps the first.

**No feature owns them: the app reads its own rows.** `Document` is an SDK entity, so the commands are a
derivation over the stored documents whose `documentType` is `commands` — there is no role to claim, no provider
to declare and nothing for a pack to serve. A pack *ships* commands by writing content, and a pack *edits* them
by editing documents. In default-setup the editor is `library`, so the documents are the user's library and they
edit them there; a second editor would need no wiring at all.

**Every window holds the list, whatever surface is open.** The app publishes it to the shell — beside which
tabs show and which surface was last open — so an editor's popup reads it from there and never from a feature's
surface. Frontend code that needs it reads `useShell().commands` (`@apackdev/sdk/fe`), or `getCommands()`
(`@apackdev/sdk/commands`) where there is no scope to follow it in. The app republishes whenever it is asked to
publish: on each connection, and after a pack is installed, updated, enabled, disabled, uninstalled or rebuilt
(the bus's `PACK_CHANGED`), or the data is replaced. Beyond that it follows the documents themselves: the SDK's
document repository announces every write and the app compares the derived list, so storing or editing a command
publishes it. One apply is one publication however many documents it wrote.

`/` is the chat input's affordance: the popup is in the `input:chat` editor and nowhere else, so a slash in a
note or a document is ordinary text.

Uninstalling a pack does not remove the commands it wrote: those documents are the user's now, so their
commands stay listed, with no flow handling them, until the user deletes them.

documents.section: Content / Slash commands / Declaring commands in the manifest
documents.body:
### Declaring commands in the manifest

```json
"extensions": {
  "commands": {
    "list": { "pr2md": { "placeholder": "PR number or GitHub URL (optional)" } },
    "onUserEdit": "offer"
  }
}
```

A command name is lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. The names are nested under `list` so that
`onUserEdit` has somewhere to sit that is not also a command name; it is optional and means here what it
means for every other entry, so leave it out for the default.

**The build desugars this into ordinary content**, compiled under the reserved key `declared-commands` as one
document holding one field per command, named after your pack id. So everything the rest of this page
describes applies unchanged: the three-way merge, removal when you stop shipping a command, offers, and the
import dialog. There is no second path for a command, and no second way the app serves one.

Your own `content.sources` keys are untouched — including the `commands` key, which is why the reserved one
is spelled differently. A pack may use both: a directory for the commands it wants to lay out as documents,
and the manifest for one or two more.

**Two things to know, because this key is weaker than it looks:**

- **It seeds commands; it does not provide them.** What a user gets is a document they own. They may edit a
  placeholder, move the document, or delete it — and a deleted one is not written back on the next boot. This
  is unlike a step type or an artifact, which exist because your pack is installed and vanish when it is not.
  If you need a command that cannot be edited away, you need a flow that handles an event, not a listed command.
- **A name another pack already uses is not refused.** Documents dedupe first-wins and silently: whichever
  document defines the name first keeps it, and yours is simply not listed. The build *does* refuse a name one
  of your **dependencies** declares, because that one is knowable while you build — across packs that know
  nothing of each other, nothing can see both, so first-wins stands.

Sending `/name args` fires a `user.command` event (`$.event.data.payload.command` is the name); there's no routing from a name to an action. To add a command:

1. Write the action that does the work (its `category` only groups it in the Actions UI).
2. Handle it in a flow: an `on("user.command", ...)` branch whose switch compares `payload.command` (`command-listener-flow.ts` for standalone commands; the Claude Code and Codex flows route `cc-*` and `cdx-*`).
3. List it, either way:
   - **a command document** — `**name**: placeholder` in one of your pack's `commands` content files, or, in the running app, one in the Library; or
   - **`extensions.commands` in your manifest** — [the shorthand](#declaring-commands-in-the-manifest), for a pack that wants a command or two without a content directory.

A command listed without a handler does nothing, and a handled command that isn't listed is sent as a plain message.

documents.body:
### Inspecting compiled references

`apack pack info` reads verified compiled content without activating a pack or importing authored
modules. Its JSON output includes each collection's `references` when its compiler supports analysis.
Flow analysis uses step declarations: `extensions.steps.<type>.dsl.references` maps a DSL field to a
compiled content key, for example `"references": { "prompt": "prompts" }`. This also works for custom
steps and nested branches exposed by their build facet.

The index records literal targets and marks computed targets as dynamic. Human-readable inspection
reports whether a literal target is indexed. A target missing from this index may still exist in user
data or be created by an applier. Analysis is static and non-exhaustive; an omitted `references` field
means analysis is unavailable, while an empty list means no known references were found. Action and
prompt JavaScript bodies are not analyzed yet.

Build tooling can use `inspectContentReferences` and `findContentDependents` from `@apackdev/sdk/build`
for missing-target and rename/removal review. These operate on index data only and never execute a
pack. Known incoming references do not rule out additional computed or runtime dependencies.

documents.body:
### Reading step declarations and implementations

Backend code reads `getStepDeclaration(type)` or `getStepDeclarations()` from
`@apackdev/sdk/steps` for labels, defaults and declared capabilities. These reads do not load pack
modules and remain available when a pack is disabled or its implementation is unavailable.
`stepRegistry.createNodeDefaults(type)` copies the declared defaults, so editing a node cannot mutate
the catalog.

Creating a node through `flowRepository` requires `getStepBinding(type)` to identify an enabled,
accepted backend matching the current declaration and build. The repository checks that binding again
after trigger validation and before writing. Missing or replaced providers refuse creation without
persisting a node. `stepRegistry.getRuntime`, `getBuild` and `getTrigger` read active providers for
execution, compilation and retirement; they do not establish eligibility for new work.

Updating a node keeps its type fixed and reads its declared relation and validation policy. A declared
trigger validator requires a matching eligible backend, checked again after validation before any write.
Missing, stale or replaced providers refuse the update. Edits with no declared validator can proceed
without activating a backend; an unknown declaration cannot establish an editing policy.

Frontend code uses `getStepDeclarations`, `getStepDeclaration` and `getStepBinding` from
`@apackdev/sdk/fe`. Frontend metadata comes from the catalog; executable views additionally require the
current frontend binding. Backend and frontend implementations have separate lifetimes.
